question: The minimum hemoglobin concentration in a fingerstick from a male blood donor is:
explanation:
The hemoglobin for women shall be ;::12.5 g/dl (hematocrit ;::38%) and the hemoglobin for
men shall be ;::13.0 g/dl (hematocrit ;::39%).
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.1.1] [AABB BBffS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.4.1A, p67]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 1 · boc1 PDF page 21

question: A cause for indefinite deferral from blood donation is:
options: a reactive test for Babesia species
residence in an endemic malaria region for 5 years
explanation:
Present or past clinical or laboratory evidence of infection with Trypanosoma cruzi
(Chagas disease) is cause for an indefinite deferral from blood donation. A reactive test for
Babesia species is a 2-year deferral, residence in a malarial endemic area for 5 years is a
3-year deferral after departure, and chicken pox vaccination is a 4-week deferral.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1.1.1] (AABB BBrrS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.4.1A, p70-73]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 2 · boc1 PDF page 21

question: Which of the following prospective donors would be accepted for blood donation?
options: 62-year-old female with a blood pressure of 210/80
82-year-old male with a hemoglobin of 13.5 g/dl
explanation:
As there is no upper age limit for blood donation and this donor's hemoglobin is ;::13.0 g/dl,
this individual is eligible to donate. All other potential donors have physical examination
requirements outside of acceptable values. Systolic blood pressure must range from
90-180 mm Hg and the diastolic blood pressure must range between 50-100 mm Hg.
Donors must weigh at least 110 lb. Pulse must be 50-100 bpm.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1.1.1] [AABB BBffS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.4.1A, p67]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 3 · boc1 PDF page 21

question: Which one of the following constitutes permanent deferral status of a donor?
options: recent close contact with a patient with viral hepatitis
2 units of blood transfused 4 months previously
confirmed positive test for HBsAg 10 years previously
explanation:
A positive test for HBsAg at any time is a permanent deferral.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1 :t.1] [AABB BBrrs Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.4.1A, p70]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 4 · boc1 PDF page 21

question:
A prospective donor with which of the following health histories would be accepted for blood
donation?
options: hepatitis B immune globulin 2 months ago
travel to malaria endemic country 1 month ago
explanation:
An individual taking HIV prevention drugs (PrEP & PEP) is eligible to donate 3 months
after the last dose. Hepatitis B immune globulin administration is a 12-month deferral. A
potential donor is deferred for 3-months after receiving a blood transfusion. Travel to a
malarial-endemic area is a 3-month deferral after departure.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.1.1] [AABB BBffS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.4.1A, p68-69, 73]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 5 · boc1 PDF page 21

question: In order to be a plateletpheresis donor, the platelet count must be at least:
explanation:
The minimum platelet count required for plateletpheresis donors is 150,000/µL.
The results of platelet counts performed before or after a procedure may be used to qualify
the donor for the next procedure.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.1.4) [AABB BBrrs Standards 2022, p22-23]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 6 · boc1 PDF page 22

question:
Prior to blood donation, the intended venipuncture site must be cleaned with a scrub solution
containing:
explanation:
The arm scrub must use povidone-iodine. Donors who are sensitive to iodine can have
the area cleaned with a preparation of 2% chlorhexidine and 70% isopropyl alcohol. Green
soap must not be used.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.1 .4] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p203-205, Method 6-2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 7 · boc1 PDF page 22

question:
A donor who has just donated 2 units of Apheresis Red Blood Cells will be deferred from
further blood donation for a minimum of how many weeks?
explanation:
Donation of 2 units of Apheresis Red Blood Cells will result in a 16-week deferral from
blood donation.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1.1.1, 1.1.1.4] [AABB BBffS Standards 2022, p23]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 8 · boc1 PDF page 22

question:
Which of the following infectious agents relies solely on donor questioning to avoid
transmission from transfused blood products?
explanation:
There are no current tests to detect the presence of Plasmodium parasites in blood
donors. Protection from transfusion-transmitted malaria relies solely on ascertaining the travel
history of prospective donors.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.1.1) [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p212; AABB BBffS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.4.1A, p72-73]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 9 · boc1 PDF page 22

question:
Which of the following practices at the time of blood collection helps minimize bacterial
contamination of platelet products?
explanation:
Diversion of the first 10-40 ml of donor blood that may contain contaminated skin into a
separate pouch helps prevent bacterial contamination in blood products. This is particularly
true of platelet products as their storage at 20-24°C can facilitate bacterial growth.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.1.5] [AABB BBffS Standards 2022, p12-13, 23; AABB Tech Manual 2020, p142, 204]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 10 · boc1 PDF page 22

question:
If a unit of autologous Red Blood Cells is collected and transfused in the same facility, which of
the following is not required?
explanation:
If the collecting and transfusing facility are the same, infectious disease screening is not
required. ABO and Rh testing must be done for each autologous donation. A physician's order
and evaluation for potential infection in the autologous donor are also required.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.1.2] [AABB BBffS Standards 2022, p20, 34, 36] [Harmening 2019, p293]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 11 · boc1 PDF page 22

question:
According to AABB Standards, what is the minimum hemoglobin level for an autologous
donor?
explanation:
Autologous blood donors must have a hemoglobin of ~11 g/dl.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.1.2) [AABB BBrrs Standards 2022, p20]
B. Processing
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 12 · boc1 PDF page 22

question:
Which of the following must be included on the label of a unit of Red Blood Cells Leukocytes
Reduced?
options: known leukocyte count for the unit
explanation:
The label on any blood product must include the unique facility identifier, such as FDA
registration number and facility name.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.2.4] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p164-165; AABB BBfTS Standards 2022, p13-14]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 13 · boc1 PDF page 22

question: All donor blood testing must include:
explanation:
Testing for syphilis was the first mandated donor screening test for infectious disease and
is still part of infectious disease testing.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.2.1] [AABB BBfTS Standards 2022, p36)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 14 · boc1 PDF page 23

question:
Which of the following is not a useful strategy to reduce bacterial contamination in platelet
components?
options: using green soap scrub to disinfect venipuncture site
diverting the first 10-40 ml of donor blood from the main blood bag
performing culture-based testing on all platelet components
applying pathogen reduction technology to platelet components
explanation:
The use of green soap to disinfect the venipuncture site is unacceptable. Products
containing povidone iodine or isopropyl alcohol and iodine tincture are suitable to prepare
the venipuncture site. Diversion of the first 10-40 ml of blood at the start of phlebotomy,
culture-based testing strategies, and pathogen reduction are all acceptable strategies to avoid
bacterial contamination in platelet components.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.2.1) [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p142, 203-205, 215]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 15 · boc1 PDF page 23

question:
Which of the following practices has been useful in reducing the incidence of transfusion
related acute lung injury (TRALI}?
options: use of Fresh Frozen Plasma from male donors
use of Fresh Frozen Plasma from female donors
pathogen reduction treatment of Fresh Frozen Plasma
explanation:
One of the mitigation strategies for Transfusion Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI) is to
use plasma components, whole blood, and platelets from male donors as they are unlikely
to demonstrate HLA antibodies. Never-pregnant female donors, or female donors who
have been found to be negative for HLA antibodies (and in some donors, negative for HNA
antibodies) since their last pregnancy, are also acceptable as donors for plasma components.
Although these measures reduce the risk of TRALI, they do not eliminate TRALI completely.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.6.3.3] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p640-643]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 16 · boc1 PDF page 23

question:
In allogeneic blood donation, which of the following infectious agents must also include a
nucleic acid testing (NAT} assay?
explanation:
Nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HBV DNA is required for each blood donation.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1.2.1] [AABB BBfTS Standards 2022. p36]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 17 · boc1 PDF page 23

question:
What is the primary reason that infectious agents can be transmitted following blood
transfusion?
options: donor in the window period of early infection
explanation:
The primary cause of residual disease transmission in the blood supply is from donors in
the window period of early infection before test results become positive.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.6.3.8] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p196-198)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 18 · boc1 PDF page 23

question: Apheresis Platelets that will undergo pathogen reduction technology do not require:
explanation:
If Apheresis Platelets undergo pathogen reduction technology, a culture-based test to
detect bacteria in the product is not required. Pathogen reduction technology is an acceptable
bacterial risk control strategy.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.2.1] [AABB BBfTS Standards 2022, p12]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 19 · boc1 PDF page 23

question:
The results in this table are obtained on a blood donor sample at immediate spin:
anti-A
anti-8
A1 cells
B cells

Before labeling blood components from this donation, what additional testing must be
completed?
options: perform weak D testing on donor RBCs
test donor serum with A2 cells
explanation:
Before labeling, weak D testing must be performed on all samples that initially test as
D-negative. If weak D testing and a control are negative, blood components are labeled as
Rh-negative. If weak D testing is positive (and the control is negative), blood components are
labeled as Rh-positive.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1.2.1] [AABB BBfTS Standards 2022, p34]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 20 · boc1 PDF page 23

question:
Which of the following courses of action must be performed immediately if a sample from an
Apheresis Platelet undergoing culture-based testing indicates bacterial growth?
options: set up another culture to confirm positivity
retrieve the unit if issued for transfusion
explanation:
Platelet components undergoing culture-based testing for the detection of bacteria are
usually released to inventory as incubation of those cultures continues. If a culture becomes
positive, the first action is to retrieve products issued from inventory as they may not
have been transfused. This retrieval can prevent an adverse reaction in a blood recipient.
Determination of the identity of the organism also needs to be done, but this can occur after
retrieval of the issued component.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.2.1] [AABB BBfTS Standards 2022, p12-13, 93]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 21 · boc1 PDF page 24

question:
A sample of blood from each donation is tested for which of the following infectious disease
agents?
options: HBsAg, HIV-1/2, P. falciparum, Babesia species
explanation:
Each blood donation is tested for HIV-1/2, HTLV-I/II, WNV, HCV, HBV, and syphilis and
can include multiple assays for each infectious agent. Depending on geographic location,
each donation may also be tested for Babesia species. Testing for Trypanosoma cruzi is a
1-time test. In May 2021 , the FDA established a policy that Zika virus is no longer a relevant
transfusion-transmitted infection and testing is no longer required.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.2.1] [AABB BBfTS Standards 2022, p36)
C. Storage
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 22 · boc1 PDF page 24

question: The transport temperature for Red Blood Cells Leukocytes Reduced is:
explanation:
The transport temperature for all red cell blood products is 1-10°C.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.3] [AABB BBfTS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p57-58]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 23 · boc1 PDF page 24

question: The transport temperature for Apheresis Platelets is:
explanation:
The transport temperature for all platelet products is 20-24°C.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1.3) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p59-61]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 24 · boc1 PDF page 24

question:
A unit of Red Blood Cells expiring in 35 days is split into 5 small aliquots using a sterile
pediatric quad set and a sterile connecting device. Each aliquot must be labeled as expiring in:
explanation:
Sterile connecting devices allow entry into donor units without affecting the expiration date
of the product.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.2.5) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, p26]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 25 · boc1 PDF page 24

question:
When platelets are stored on a rotator set on an open bench top, the ambient air temperature
must be recorded:
explanation:
If storage devices do not have automated temperature recording, ambient temperature
must be monitored and recorded every 4 hours.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.3] [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, p16]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 26 · boc1 PDF page 24

question: Which of the following is the correct storage temperature for the component listed?
explanation:
Fresh Frozen Plasma is stored at~ 18°C for 12 months.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.3] [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p63]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 27 · boc1 PDF page 24

question:
Six units of Red Blood Cells are issued to the OR at 9 AM in a cooler, validated to maintain a
temperature of 1-10°C for 2 hours. The cooler containing the units of blood is returned to the
blood bank 40 minutes later because surgery is cancelled. What should be done with these
units?
options: discard the units as they were issued to a specific patient
inspect units and establish that appropriate temperature has been maintained
continue to store in cooler since surgery is rescheduled for tomorrow
put units back into inventory as only 40 minutes has elapsed since issue
explanation:
Blood may be returned to the blood bank after issue provided that 1) the container closure
has not been disturbed, 2) at least 1 sealed segment is attached to the container, 3) visual
inspection of the unit is satisfactory and documented, and 4) the unit has been maintained at
the appropriate storage or transport temperature.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.5.1.8.1] [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, p48]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 28 · boc1 PDF page 24

question: An acceptable storage temperature for Red Blood Cells, Frozen is:
explanation:
Red Blood Cells Frozen with 40% glycerol are stored at S-65°C.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.3) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p58]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 29 · boc1 PDF page 25

question: Red Blood Cells, Leukocytes Reduced must be stored at:
explanation:
Red Blood Cells, Leukocytes Reduced are stored at 1-6°C.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.3) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p58]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 30 · boc1 PDF page 25

question:
If the seal is entered or broken on a unit of Red Blood Cells stored at 1-6°C, what is the
maximum allowable storage period, in hours?
explanation:
If the seal is broken or entered during processing or storage, components are considered
to be in an open system, rather than a closed system. The expiration time for Red Blood Cells
in an open system is 24 hours.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.4) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p57]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 31 · boc1 PDF page 25

question: Cryoprecipitated AHF must be stored at:
explanation:
Cryoprecipitated AHF is stored at ~18°C.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.3] [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p62]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 32 · boc1 PDF page 25

question:
Plasma Frozen Within 24 Hours After Phlebotomy (PF24) and thawed for transfusion has an
expiration of:
explanation:
Plasma Frozen Within 24 Hours After Phlebotomy and thawed has an expiration of 24
hours.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.4) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p63]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 33 · boc1 PDF page 25

question: Apheresis Platelets must be stored at:
explanation:
Apheresis Platelets are stored at 20-24 °C.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.3) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p60]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 34 · boc1 PDF page 25

question: Cryoprecipitated AHF, if maintained in the frozen state at - 18°C or below, has a shelf life of:
explanation:
Cryoprecipitated AHF has a shelf life of 12 months if stored at s-18°C in the frozen state.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.1 .4) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1 .BA, p62]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 35 · boc1 PDF page 25

question: Thawed Plasma must be stored at:
explanation:
Thawed Plasma is stored at 1-6°C.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.3) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p64]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 36 · boc1 PDF page 25

question: During storage, the concentration of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) decreases in a unit of:
explanation:
2,3-DPG declines during storage of Red Blood Cells, causing a "shift-to-the-left" in the
oxygen dissociation curve and an impaired ability to deliver oxygen to the tissues.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.2.2] [Harmening 2019, p8-9]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 37 · boc1 PDF page 25

question:
Upon inspection, a unit of Apheresis Platelets is noted to have visible clots, but otherwise
appears normal. The technologist should:
options: centrifuge to express off the clots
quarantine for Gram stain and culture
explanation:
Clots in the unit may indicate bacterial contamination. Other visible signs of possible
contamination could include particulate matter, discoloration of the product, and bubbles/
frothiness.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.5.1.1, 1.6.3. 7) [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p522]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 38 · boc1 PDF page 26

question:
Upon expiration, a unit of thawed Plasma Frozen Within 24 Hours (PF24) is converted to
thawed Plasma. This thawed Plasma can be stored for an additional:
explanation:
Thawed Plasma has an expiration date of 5 days from the date the product is thawed.
This product was already thawed for 24 hours, leaving 4 days before expiration.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.4) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p65]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 39 · boc1 PDF page 26

question:
The transfusion service is preparing aliquots from a unit of Red Blood Cells Leukocytes
Reduced with the aid of a sterile connecting device for a pediatric patient. When checking the
weld for one of these aliquots, it is noted that the weld is incomplete and leaking. This unit is
then resealed with an acceptable weld. What will the expiration date of this unit be?
explanation:
Since the original weld for this unit was incomplete, this product was prepared in an open
system. The expiration date will be 24 hours.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.4) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p58]
D. Blood Components
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 40 · boc1 PDF page 26

question:
A patient with a platelet count of 10,000/µL receives one unit of Apheresis Platelets,
Leukocytes Reduced. After transfusion, the patient's platelet count is 50,000/µL. These results
indicate:
options: The presence of HLA antibodies and refractoriness to transfusion
The patient is actively bleeding but still producing platelets
The platelet count is the expected posttransfusion increment
The patient's pre-transfusion platelet count was incorrect
explanation:
Each Apheresis Platelets, Leukocytes Reduced will increase the platelet count by
approximately 30,000-50,000/µL in a 70-kg adult. Lesser increases suggest refractoriness
that may be immune in origin including the presence of HLA-antibodies or clinical
refractoriness, such as DIC, bleeding, and sepsis.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.4] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p565]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 41 · boc1 PDF page 26

question:
Red Blood Cells Leukocytes Reduced must be prepared by a method known to reduce the
leukocyte count to:
explanation:
The method used to produce Red Blood Cells Leukocytes Reduced must assure <5.0 x
106 residual leukocytes per unit.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.5) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, p28-29]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 42 · boc1 PDF page 26

question:
A unit of Red Blood Cells that expires in 32 days has just been irradiated. The expiration date
of this unit will:
explanation:
When red blood cell products are irradiated, the expiration date will be the original date or
28 days from the date of irradiation, whichever is sooner.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.4.1] [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p58]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 43 · boc1 PDF page 26

question:
Cryoprecipitated AHF must be transfused within what period of time following thawing and
pooling without the use of a sterile connection device?
explanation:
Cryoprecipitated AHF must be transfused within 4 hours after thawing and pooling in an
open system. If thawed and then pooled using a sterile connection, the expiration time is 6
hours.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.4] [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p62]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 44 · boc1 PDF page 26

question:
According to AABB Standards, Fresh Frozen Plasma must be infused within what period of
time following thawing?
explanation:
Per AABB Standards, thawed Fresh Frozen Plasma should be stored at 1-6°C for no
more than 24 hours.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.4] [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p63]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 45 · boc1 PDF page 27

question: Cryoprecipitated AHF:
options: should be stored at 4°C prior to administration
will not transmit hepatitis B virus
is indicated for the treatment of hemophilia B
explanation:
Cryoprecipitated AHF is used primarily for fibrinogen replacement. It is stored at room
temperature (20-24°C) after thawing and must be infused within 6 hours as single units or
if pooled using a sterile connecting device. If pooled in an open system, it must be infused
within 4 hours.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.4] [Harmening 2019, p362; AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.BA, p62]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 46 · boc1 PDF page 27

question: Which Apheresis Platelets product should be irradiated?
options: autologous unit collected prior to surgery
random stock unit going to a patient with DIC
a directed donation given by a mother for her son
a directed donation given by an unrelated family friend
explanation:
Blood products from blood relatives containing viable lymphocytes must be irradiated to
inhibit the proliferation of T cells and prevent transfusion-associated GVHD.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.6.3.2] [Harmening 2019, p385-387]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 47 · boc1 PDF page 27

question: Irradiation of a unit of Red Blood Cells is done to prevent the replication of donor:
explanation:
Irradiation inhibits proliferation of donor T lymphocytes and renders them
immunoincompetent and unable to cause transfusion-associated GVHD.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.6.3.2] [Harmening 2019, p385-387]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 48 · boc1 PDF page 27

question:
Plastic bag overwraps are recommended when thawing units of FFP in 37°C water baths
because they prevent:
options: the FFP bag from cracking when it contacts the warm water
water from slowly dialyzing across the bag membrane
the entry ports from becoming contaminated with water
the label from peeling off as the water circulates in the bath
explanation:
FFP thawed in a water bath should be protected with a plastic overwrap so that entry
ports are not contaminated with water. FDA-cleared dry-thawing devices may also be used to
thaw FFP and do not require a protective overwrap.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.4] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p156]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 49 · boc1 PDF page 27

question: Which of the following blood components must be prepared within 8 hours after phlebotomy?
explanation:
Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) must be separated and frozen within 8 hours of Whole Blood
collection.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.1.4) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, Reference Standard 5.1.8A, p63]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 50 · boc1 PDF page 27

question: Which of the following is proper procedure for preparation of Platelets from Whole Blood?
options: light spin followed by a hard spin
light spin followed by 2 hard spins
hard spin followed by a light spin
explanation:
Whole blood-derived Platelets are prepared by a light spin to separate the Red Blood
Cells from the platelet-rich plasma (PRP), followed by a heavy spin of the PRP to concentrate
the platelets.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.1.2.2] [Harmening 2019, p337-339]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 51 · boc1 PDF page 27

question:
Of the following blood components, which one should be used to prevent HLA
alloimmunization of the recipient?
explanation:
Leukoreduction of blood products reduces donor leukocytes to less than 5 x 106
leukocytes per unit. and decreases the risk of HLA alloimmunization.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1.5, 1.6.3.5] [Harmening 2019, p339-340]
E. Blood Component Quality Control
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 52 · boc1 PDF page 27

question:
Quality control of Apheresis Granulocytes must demonstrate which of the following granulocyte
counts in 75% of units tested?
explanation:
Apheresis Granulocytes must yield a minimum of 1.0 x 1010 granulocytes in at least
75% of units tested.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1.5) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, p34]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 53 · boc1 PDF page 28

question: An important determinant of platelet viability during storage is:
explanation:
The pH of all platelet products should be maintained at 6.2 or above throughout the
storage period.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.1.5) [AABB BB/TS Standards 2022, p31-33]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 54 · boc1 PDF page 28

question:

7 .5 x 1010 platelets per unit in 100% of the units tested
8.5 x 1010 platelets per unit in 95% of the units tested

question:
Most blood group system genes and their resulting genetic traits display what type of
inheritance?
explanation:
Most blood group genes are autosomal; the XG blood group is found on the X
chromosome. Whenever a blood group gene is inherited, the antigen (the trait) is expressed
on the red blood cells, and is known as codominant inheritance.

is expressed in the formula p + q = 1.0. p2 is the homozygous population of Jk8, or those who

question:
In a random population, 16% of the people are Rh-negative (rr). What percentage of the
Rh-positive population is heterozygous for r1
explanation:
The Hardy-Weinberg equation states p + q= 1.0. When the equation is expanded, it is
p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1.0. p2 equals those that are homozygous for D, 2pq equals those that are
heterozygous for D and q2 represents those that are D-negative (rr). Homozygous population
that is D-negative equals 0.16 (rr).The square root of 0.16 is 0.4 (q) and p can be determined
by subtracting q from 1 where p equals 0.6 (0.4+0.6=1 .0). Use this in the expanded equation
to determine the D-positive population that is heterozygous for D, or 2pq or 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48
or48%.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.1.2] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p276-278]

explanation:

question:
Which of the following phenotypes is the result of homozygous inheritance of the
corresponding genes?
explanation:
Homozygous is the term used when identical alleles at a given locus are inherited.
The Fy(a-b+) phenotype may be the result of Fyb Fyb genotype. M+N+ and Jk(a+b+) would
result from inheriting non-identical alleles at a given locus, which is termed heterozygous.
LE antigens are not the result of codominant alleles, but rather the interactions of 2 genes,
Le and Se, at different loci.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.2.1.1) [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p266-268, 314]

question: What do the Oh (Classical Bombay), group 0, and Lu(a-b-) phenotypes have in common?
options: result from inheritance of identical sex-linked dominant genes
result from inheritance of identical sex-linked recessive genes
result from inheritance of identical autosomal dominant genes
result from inheritance of identical autosomal recessive genes
explanation:
These are all examples of blood group phenotypes that arise from the inheritance of
2 autosomal recessive genes. The Oh phenotype results from the inheritance of 2 "h" genes
(nonfunctional FUT1 and nonfunctional FUT2 genes). The group O phenotype results from
the inheritance of 2 recessive O genes and the Lu(a-b-) phenotype from the inheritance of
2 recessive LU genes.
(QCMLS 2021:1.2.1.1] [Harmening 2019, p28, 134]

A blood donor has the genotype: hh, AB. Using anti-A and anti-B antisera, the donor's red cells

The father has the phenotype D+C+E-c+e+. The baby is Rh-negative and not affected with
hemolytic disease of the newborn. What is the baby's most probable Rh genotype?
explanation:
The baby is D-negative and also c-negative as there is no evidence of HDFN. The gene

antibody most likely to develop would be anti-c.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.6.2) [Harmening 2019, p155-157]

question: The red cells of a nonsecretor (se/se) will most likely type as:
explanation:
The LE antigens are developed by gene interaction. Both the LE and SE gene are
required for red cells to type as Le(a-b+). If a person has a LE gene, but not a SE gene, then
the cells type as Le(a+b-). The Le(a-b-) phenotype is derived when the LE gene is absent
and the SE gene may or may not be present. The Le(a+b-) phenotype occurs in 22% of the
population, and Le(a-b-) occurs in 6%, so the most likely phenotype of a nonsecretor (se/se)
is Le(a+b-).

question: Which of the following antibodies is neutralizable by pooled human plasma?
explanation:

found as a soluble substance in plasma and capable of attaching to the surface of red blood
cells. Neutralization studies with pooled plasma containing CH/RG substance can help
confirm the antibody reactivity in a patient's sample. If test procedures are performed to coat

hemolytic transfusion reactions?

question: HLA antibodies are:
explanation:
HLA antibodies are formed in response to pregnancy, transfusion or transplantation
and are therefore not naturally occurring. They are associated with febrile nonhemolytic
transfusion reactions, refractoriness to platelet transfusions, and TRALI. They are directed
against antigens found on platelets and most other nucleated cells in the body.

are linked to genes in the ABO system

contribute to the coordination of cellular and humoral immunity
----------'---
explanation:
MHC consists of both class I and class II HLA antigens. Discrimination of self from
non-self, immune response to antigenic stimuli, and the coordination of cellular and humeral

explanation:
The M and N antigens are found on glycophorin A. The S and s antigens are found on
glycophorin B.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.2.7.1] (Harmening 2019, p189]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 103 · boc1 PDF page 35

question:
Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH) is associated with antibody specificity toward which of
the following?
explanation:
Autoanti-P, a cold-reactive lgG autoantibody described as a biphasic hemolysin, is
associated with paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.4.2.4.1] (Harmening 2019, p184]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 104 · boc1 PDF page 36

question: Which of the following is a characteristic of anti-i?
options: associated with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
found in the serum of patients with infectious mononucleosis
detected at lower temperatures in the serum of normal individuals
found only in the serum of group O individuals
explanation:
Patients with infectious mononucleosis often demonstrate potent examples of anti-i that
are transient in nature.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.4.2.3] [Harmening 2019, p186]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 105 · boc1 PDF page 36

question:
In a case of cold agglutinin disease, the patient's serum would most likely react 4+ at
immediate spin with:
options: group A cells, B cells and O cells, but not his own cells
cord cells but not his own or other adult cells
all cells of a group O cell panel and his own cells
only penicillin-treated panel cells, not his own cells
explanation:
Anti-I is an autoantibody commonly found in all individuals, but when it causes hemolysis,
the titer may be high and have a broad thermal range with reactivity at 30°C or higher. Cold
agglutinin disease can be associated with M. pneumoniae infection and in lymphoproliferative
diseases.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.4.2.3.1] [Harmening 2019, p447-451]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 106 · boc1 PDF page 36

question:
Cold agglutinin disease is associated with an antibody specificity toward which of
the following?
explanation:
Anti-I is associated with cold agglutinin disease.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.4.2.3.1] [ Harmening 2019, p447-451]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 107 · boc1 PDF page 36

question: Which of the following is a characteristic of anti-i?
options: often associated with hemolytic disease of the newborn
reacts best at room temperature or 4°C
explanation:
Anti-i is an lgM antibody that reacts with cord cells and i adult cells. It is not associated
with hemolytic disease of the newborn since lgM antibodies do not cross the placenta.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.2.4.1] [ Harmening 2019, p447-451]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 108 · boc1 PDF page 36

question:
In chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), granulocyte function is impaired. An association
exists between this clinical condition and a depression of which of the following antigens?
explanation:
Red blood cells of individuals with the McLeod phenotype lack Kx and Km and have
significant depression of other KEL antigens. The McLeod phenotype has been found in
patients with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD).
(QCMLS 2021: 1.2.8.1] [Harmening 2019, p196-197)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 109 · boc1 PDF page 36

question: The antibodies of the JK blood group system:
options: react best by the indirect antiglobulin test
do not generally react with antigen-positive, enzyme-treated RBCs
explanation:
Antibodies in the JK blood group system are lgG and react best at the antiglobulin phase.
These antibodies are associated with delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions and reactivity
can be enhanced by testing with enzyme-pretreated cells.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.10.1] [Harmening 2019, p200]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 110 · boc1 PDF page 36

question: Proteolytic enzyme treatment of red cells usually destroys which antigen?
explanation:
The Fya and Fyb antigens are sensitive to denaturation by proteolytic enzymes.
Serum containing anti-Fy8 reacts with untreated Fy(a+) cells, but not with enzyme-treated
Fy(a+) cells. The Jka, E and k antigens are not destroyed by proteolytic enzymes.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.2.9.1] [Harmening 2019, p198]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 111 · boc1 PDF page 36

question: Anti-Fy8 is:
options: more reactive when tested with enzyme-treated red blood cells
capable of causing hemolytic transfusion reactions
explanation:
Anti-Fya is an lgG antibody that reacts best at the AHG phase, does not react with
enzyme-treated red cells, is capable of causing hemolytic disease of the newborn, and is not
known to be an autoagglutinin.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.9.2] [Harmening 2019, p198]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 112 · boc1 PDF page 36

question: Resistance to malaria is best associated with which of the following blood groups?
explanation:
The FY glycoprotein on red cells is a receptor for the malarial parasite Plasmodium vivax.
Red cells with the phenotype Fy(a-b-) are resistant to invasion by P. vivax.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.2.9.1] [Harmening 2019, p196]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 113 · boc1 PDF page 37

question: What is linkage disequilibrium in reference to HLA haplotypes?
options:
occurrence of HLA genes in the same haplotype more often than would be expected based
on the gene frequencies
displacement of HLA genes on different chromosomes

occurrence of HLA genes in the same haplotype less often than would be expected based
on the gene frequencies
recombination of HLA genes during meiosis
explanation:
Linkage disequilibrium results when genes occur more frequently in a haplotype than is
expected based on chance alone. This is commonly seen in the HLA system and the MNS
blood group system.
(QCMLS 2021: 8.1.1.3] [Harmening 2019, p187, 501)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 114 · boc1 PDF page 37

What is the most probable genotype of this patient?
explanation:
After performing rule outs, the most likely antibody is anti-c. To form anti-c, the patient
would need to inherit a gene from both parents that does not produce the c antigen.
Individuals with the R1R1 or r'r' genotype would lack the c antigen but the r'r' genotype is
very rare.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.6.2] [Harmening 2019, p156]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 115 · boc1 PDF page 37

question: Antibodies produced to blood group antigens that are carbohydrate structures are usually:
explanation:
Blood groups with carbohydrate antigens include ABO, H, LE, I, P1 PK and GLOB.
Antibodies to these antigens are usually naturally occurring, lgM, direct agglutinins and react
best at room temperature.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.2.1] [Harmening 2019, p62]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 116 · boc1 PDF page 37

question: Which of the following red blood cells would lack the Lu3 antigen?
explanation:
Lu3 is a high-prevalence antigen found on all red cells except those of the rare Lu(a-b-)
phenotype.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.2.11] [Harmening 2019, p204]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 117 · boc1 PDF page 37

question: Which of the following is considered a low-prevalence antigen?
explanation:
Wr8 is a low-prevalence antigen. Low-prevalence antigens are those that occur in
<10% of the population. Yt8 and Oib are both high-prevalence antigens, occurring in >98% of
the population. Jkb is neither a high-prevalence nor a low-prevalence antigen, occurring in
approximately 74% of the white population and 48% of the black population.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.2.13, 1.2.1 OJ
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 118 · boc1 PDF page 37

question: Which of the following statement is correct?
options: antibodies to high-prevalence antigens are most often lgM and room temperature reactive
antibodies to high-prevalence antigens are usually clinically significant
antibodies to high-prevalence antigens occur in >98% of the population
antibodies to high-prevalence antigens include examples of anti-K
explanation:
Antibodies to high-prevalence antigens are usually immune in origin, clinically significant,
lgG, bind to their respective antigens at 37°C and are reactive at the antiglobulin phase
of testing. High-prevalence antigens occur in >98% of the population, but antibodies to
high-prevalence antigens are uncommon. Anti-K is a commonly encountered alloantibody
and the K antigen is not a high-prevalence antigen, as it is present on the red cells
of approximately 9% of the population.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.13]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 119 · boc1 PDF page 38

question: For which of the following is HLA phenotyping not useful?
options: selection of bone marrow donor for transplantation
investigation of a hemolytic transfusion reaction
selection of solid organ donor for transplantation
investigation of platelet refractoriness in transfusion recipient
explanation:
Platelets express HLA Class I antigens. Antibodies to these antigens may be the cause of
platelet refractoriness. Both bone marrow and solid organ transplantation require donor and
recipient matching for select HLA antigens. A hemolytic transfusion reaction is the result of
recipient antibodies directed against donor red cell antigens and is unrelated to HLA antigens.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.15] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p491 , 493-495)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 120 · boc1 PDF page 38

question: Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT) is:
options: frequently caused by maternal HLA antibodies
frequently caused by maternal anti-HPA-1a antibodies
treated with IVIG and washed paternal platelets
explanation:
Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT) results from platelet
destruction due to anti-HPA antibodies. The most implicated specificity is anti-HPA-1a. IVIG is
a treatment for FNAIT and could be paired with maternal washed platelets transfused to the
affected fetus or neonate. The father can be assumed to be positive for the HPA-1a or other
HPA antigen responsible for FNAIT and would not be an appropriate source for transfused
platelets to the affected fetus or neonate.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.15.2] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p464]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 121 · boc1 PDF page 38

question: Which of the following statement regarding the LW blood group system is true?
options: D-negative red cells express more LW antigen than 0-positive red cells
Rhnull red cells are also LW(a-b-)
LW antibodies generally react at the room temperature (RT) phase of testing
the LW system has 3 antigens: low-prevalence LW8 and high-prevalence LWb and LWab
explanation:
Rhnull red cells are also LW(a-b-). 0-positive cells express more LW antigen than
D-negative cells. LW antibodies usually react at the indirect antiglobulin phase of testing.
LWb is the low-prevalence antigen and Lwa and Lwab are high-prevalence antigens.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.12] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p275-277]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 122 · boc1 PDF page 38

question: In which of the following conditions are HNA antibodies not implicated?
explanation:
TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) is a complication of transfusion
resulting from volume overload and is not immunologic in origin. AIN can be seen in infants or
adults. In infants, the autoantibody specificity is usually anti-HNA-1 a. TRALI is a transfusion
adverse event that can be initiated by HLA and HNA antibodies that are present in the donor's
blood. NAN is caused by maternal lgG HNA antibodies.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.2.15.3] [AABB Tech Manual 2020, p425-428 and 582-585)
C. Role of Blood Groups in Transfusion
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 123 · boc1 PDF page 38

Anti-K is identified in a patient's serum. If random crossmatches are performed on 10 donor
units, approximately how many would be expected to be compatible?
explanation:
The K antigen is absent in 91 % of the White population and 98% of the Black population.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.8.1] [Harmening 2019, p194-195]

question:
Four units of blood are needed for elective surgery. The patient's serum contains anti-C, anti-e,
anti-Fy8 and anti-Jkb. Which of the following would be the best source of donor blood?
options: test all units in current stock
explanation:
The frequency of compatible donors for this patient can be calculated by multiplying
the percentage of the population that is e- x C- x Fy(a-) x Jk(b-). In the random White
population, 2% are e-, 32% are C-, 32% are Fy(a-) and 26% are Jk(b-). Multiplication shows
that finding compatible units will be rare (.05 units per 100 units) and random screening for
compatible units would be a challenge. The blood supplier's immunohematology reference
laboratory (IRL) may have units in stock or can request blood from other IRLs through the
rare donor registry.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.14.2] [Harmening 2019, p248]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 125 · boc1 PDF page 38

question:
A patient is group 0, Rh-negative with anti-0 and anti-Kin her serum. What percentage of the
general Caucasian donor population would be compatible with this patient?
explanation:
Determination of compatibility can be determined by multiplying the percentage of
compatibility of each antigen. 45% of the population is group 0 , 15% are D-negative, and
91 % are K-negative. 0.45 x 0.15 x 0.91 = 0.06, or 6%.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.14.2) [Harmening 2019, p248]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 126 · boc1 PDF page 38

question: Which of the following Rh antigens has the highest frequency in Caucasians?
explanation:
The overall incidence of thee antigen is 98%. The overall incidence of c is 80%, D is 85%
and Eis 30%.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.2.6.1) [Harmening 2019, p158]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 127 · boc1 PDF page 39

question: The K (KEL 1) antigen is:
options: absent from the red cells of neonates
has a frequency of 50% in the random population
explanation:
The K antigen is highly immunogenic. It is present on the red cells of up to 9% of adults
and neonates and is not affected by enzymes.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.2.8.2] [Harmening 2019, p194-195]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 128 · boc1 PDF page 39

question:
What percent of group O donors would be compatible with a serum sample that contained
anti-X and anti-Y if X antigen is present on red cells of 5 of 20 donors, and Y antigen is present
on red cells of 1 of 1 O donors?
explanation:
75% of donors would be compatible with anti-X and 90% with anti-Y. The frequency of
compatibility for both antigens is determined by multiplying the 2 compatibility percentages:
0.75 x 0.90 = 0.675 or 68%.
[QCMLS 2021:1.2.14.2) [Harmening 2019, p248]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 129 · boc1 PDF page 39

question:
What is the approximate probability of finding compatible blood among random Rh-positive
units for a patient who has anti-c and anti-K? (Consider that 20% of Rh-positive donors lack c
and 90% lack K)
explanation:
Multiplication of the individual compatibility frequencies results in the percentage of
compatible donors that would lack both antigens. 0.20 x 0.90 = 0.18, or 18%.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.14.2] (Harmening 2019, 248]
Ill. Blood Group Immunology
A. Immune Response
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 130 · boc1 PDF page 39

question: Which of the following is responsible for the production of blood group antibodies?
explanation:
B lymphocytes (B cells) mature in the bone marrow and evolve into plasma cells that
secrete antibody when stimulated by antigen. Plasma cells and resulting memory B cells are
an integral part of humoral immunity.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.1) [Harmening 2019, p50-51]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 131 · boc1 PDF page 39

question: In a primary immune response, which immunoglobulin class appears first?
explanation:
During a primary response, lgM antibodies are the first to be produced, followed by the
production of lgG antibodies.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.3.1) [Harmening 2019, p52]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 132 · boc1 PDF page 39

question: What is the most common clinical incident that results in alloantibody production?
explanation:
Alloimmunization resulting in the production of blood group antibodies is associated
with red cell transfusions. Exposure to foreign red blood cell antigens from pregnancy or
transplantation may also result in alloantibody production.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.1] [Harmening 2019, p62-63]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 133 · boc1 PDF page 39

question: Macrophages and monocytes have Fe receptors for which of the following immunoglobulins?
explanation:
Macrophages and monocytes have receptors for the Fe portion of lgG molecules. This
is one of the ways that lgG sensitized red cells are removed from the circulatory system and
phagocytized.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.4.25.1.2] [Harmening 2019, p59; AABB Tech Manual 2020, p246-247]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 134 · boc1 PDF page 39

question:
Which of the following blood group antigens is the most immunogenic, or has the greatest
ability to initiate antibody production in an individual who lacks the antigen?
explanation:
The most immunogenic blood group antigen is D (Rh0). If D-negative individuals are
exposed to even small amounts of D-positive red blood cells, anti-D will be produced in a
significant number of individuals.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.6) [Harmening 2019, p62, 158]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 135 · boc1 PDF page 40

question:
lgG antibody and/or C3b sensitized red blood cells can be phagocytized by cells in the
reticuloendothelial system (RES). This phenomenon is clinically recognized as:
explanation:
Removal of lgG and/or C3b-sensitized red blood cells by the RES system can be noted
as extravascular hemolysis and a delayed transfusion reaction.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.4.2.1.2] [Harmening 2019, p61; AABB Tech Manual 2020, p247]
B. lmmunog/obulins
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 136 · boc1 PDF page 40

question: Which immunoglobulin class can cross the placenta?
explanation:
Only lgG antibodies can cross the placenta.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.2] [Harmening 2019, p55, 58]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 137 · boc1 PDF page 40

question:
Which of the following immunoglobulins is most efficient at activating complement via the
classical pathway?
explanation:
lgM is a large molecule with 5 Fe monomers in close proximity, facilitating the activation of
complement via the classical pathway.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.3.2] [Harmening 2019, p57, 59-61]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 138 · boc1 PDF page 40

question: Which of the following immunoglobulins is most efficient at causing direct hemagglutination?
explanation:
Each lgM molecule has 10 Fab sites, or antigen binding sites. This allows this molecule to
attach to multiple antigen sites on adjacent red blood cells, facilitating direct hemagglutination.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.3.2] [Harmening 2019, p55, 57, 67]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 139 · boc1 PDF page 40

question:
Which of the following structures of an immunoglobulin molecule is involved in the activation of
complement via the classical pathway?
explanation:
Binding of complement C1 protein to the Fe fragment of an immunoglobulin molecule
initiates the activation of complement via the classical pathway.
[QCMLS 2021: 8.1.4.1) [Harmening 2019, p59]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 140 · boc1 PDF page 40

question: lmmunoglobulin classes are differentiated according to the molecular structure of:
explanation:
lg classes are differentiated based on their amino acid sequences of the constant region
of the heavy chains.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.3.2] [Harmening 2019, p55-56; AABB Tech Manual 2020, p243-246]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 141 · boc1 PDF page 40

question:
Which of the following pairs of immunoglobulins is most efficient at activating complement via
the classical pathway?
explanation:
The lgG1 and lgG3 subclasses of lgG are the most efficient at activating complement via
the classical pathway.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.2] [Harmening 2019, 58-59]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 142 · boc1 PDF page 40

To evaluate potential risk to the fetus, what additional studies should be performed?
options: test additional cells to rule-out anti-c
treat serum with dithiothreitol and repeat panel
perform D testing on father's blood
explanation:
This red cell antibody identification panel depicts anti-M. While usually lgM, this antibody
may also be lgG and the reactions observed suggest that the antibody may have an lgG
component. Treating the serum with sulfhydryl reagents such as dithiothreitol (OTT) will
cleave lgM molecules, rendering them nonreactive. OTT has no effect on lgG molecules.
As only lgG antibodies are capable of placental transfer, it is important to determine if this
antibody is lgM, lgG, or a mixture of both.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.4.1.2.1] [Harmening 2019, p57, 432]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 143 · boc1 PDF page 41

question:
The immune response to red cell antigens with numerous epitopes results in a heterogeneous
population of antibodies referred to as:
explanation:
B cells, when stimulated, produce antibodies to multiple epitopes on an antigen.
The different epitopes on a single antigen induce proliferation of different B cells clones
that result in a heterogeneous population of antibodies. These antibodies are referred to as
polyclonal.
(QCMLS 2021 : 8.1.2.5] [Harmening 2019, p61-62]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 144 · boc1 PDF page 41

question:
A blood sample is taken from a 90-year-old male, who is admitted to the ER for possible
GI bleeding. ABO results are shown in this table:
cells tested with
serum tested with
anti-A

What might be a likely explanation for these results?
explanation:
Various host factors play a role in an individual's immune response and one of those
factors is age. A decrease in antibody levels may be seen in older individuals and may result
in a false-negative reaction as seen in reverse ABO typing.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.2.2.5] (Harmening 2019, p64]
C. Antigen-Antibody Interactions
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 145 · boc1 PDF page 41

question:
Appropriate antigen-antibody ratios are important to avoid an excess of unbound antibody,
which is known as:
explanation:
Excess antibody, known as prozone, may lead to false-negative agglutination results.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.3.4] [Harmening 2019, p66]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 146 · boc1 PDF page 41

question:
Many enhancement media used in the blood bank promote hemagglutination in the presence
of lgG antibodies by reducing which of the following?
explanation:
Many enhancement media promote hemagglutination by reducing the zeta potential. Red
blood cells naturally repel each other due to the net negative charge that surrounds each cell.
A potential is created because of the cations (positively charged ions) that are attracted to
the zone of negative charges. This potential is the zeta potential. Reducing the zeta potential
allows the more positively charged antibodies to get closer to the negatively charged red
cells, facilitating agglutination.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.3] [Harmening 2019, p67-68]

question:
Blood group antigen and antibody hemagglutination reactions are influenced by which of the
following?
explanation:
Several factors influence hemagglutination reactions including antigen-antibody ratio, pH,
temperature, enhancement media and the use of anti-human globulin reagents.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.3.4] [Harmening 2019, p66-67]

question:
Which of the following blood group antibodies will no longer react with its respective antigens
once those antigens are treated with proteolytic enzymes?
explanation:
The Fya, Fyb, M, and N antigens are destroyed when red cells are treated with proteolytic
enzymes. The S antigen may be destroyed or weakened when red cells are treated with
proteolytic enzymes.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.5.3] [Harmening 2019, p?O]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 149 · boc1 PDF page 42

question:
Some blood group antibodies may react stronger with the red cells of individuals who have
inherited 2 identical alleles for the antigen to which the antibody is directed. This is known as:
explanation:
Dosage effect reflects different amounts of antigen expressed on the red cell surface.
For example, an individual that inherits 2 identical MM genes will express more M antigen
than an individual of the genotype MN. Some examples of anti-M will react stronger with red
cells that are MM vs red cells that are MN.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.5.1.9] [Harmening 2019, p66]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 150 · boc1 PDF page 42

question:
Which of the following reagents is used to facilitate hemagglutination following the sensitization
of red cells with an lgG alloantibody?
explanation:
Anti-human globulin serum will facilitate hemagglutination of red blood cells sensitized
with lgG antibody.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.3.5] [Harmening 2019, p70, 104]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 151 · boc1 PDF page 42

question:
The addition of antibody-sensitized red cells (Check Cells) to all negative anti-human globulin
(AHG) tests ensures that:
options: the test was incubated at the correct temperature
AHG reagent was added to each test
patient serum was added to each test
explanation:
All negative antiglobulin tests must be verified with the addition of lgG-sensitized RBCs
(Check Cells). Failure to demonstrate hemagglutination following the addition of lgGsensitized RBCs invalidates the test and suggests the possibility of inadequate washing to
remove unbound globulin, failure to add AHG reagent, or faulty/nonreactive AHG.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.5] [Harmening 2019, p114]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 152 · boc1 PDF page 42

question: In which of the following clinical situations will the direct antiglobulin test be positive?
options: hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
explanation:
Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn will demonstrate a positive direct
antiglobulin test.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.4.1.2.2] [Harmening 2019, p109-111]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 153 · boc1 PDF page 42

question: In which of the following is the indirect antiglobulin test utilized?
explanation:
Following incubation at 37°C, antibody detection (screening) tests must include an indirect
antiglobulin phase to facilitate detection of clinically significant antibodies.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.3.5] [Harmening 2019, p112-114;AABB BB/TS Standards, 2022, p40]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 154 · boc1 PDF page 42

question: PolyspecificAHG reagents contain:
explanation:
Polyspecific AHG reagents must contain anti-lgG and anti-C3d. Monospecific AHG
reagents contain only one antibody specificity and can include anti-lgG, anti-C3d and
anti-C3b.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.5] [Harmening 2019, p104-108]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 155 · boc1 PDF page 43

question: A false-negative direct antiglobulin test can be the result of:
explanation:
Neutralized AHG reagent, no longer able to bind to lgG immunoglobulin, can result in a
false-negative test result.
[Harmening 2019, p114]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 156 · boc1 PDF page 43

question: A false-positive indirect antiglobulin test can be the result of:
options: insufficient saline washing of red cells
explanation:
Overcentrifugation of the test can result in a false-positive result.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.5] [Harmening 2019, p114]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 157 · boc1 PDF page 43

question: A negative result using solid phase adherence assays will demonstrate indicator red cells as:
options: a red blood cell pellet in the bottom of the well
a diffuse pattern of red blood cells throughout the well
red blood cell clumps symmetrically located throughout the well
explanation:
Negative reactions using solid-phase technology will appear as a button at the center of
the microplate well following centrifugation.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.6] [Harmening 2019, p272-276]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 158 · boc1 PDF page 43

question: A 4+ positive reactions using gel technology will appear as red blood cells:
options: in a pellet at the bottom of the microtubule
in a layer at the top of the gel media
suspended at the mid-point of the gel media
explanation:
A 4+ reaction using gel technology will appear as a solid band of agglutinated cells at the
top of the gel column.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.6] [Harmening 2019, p269-276]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 159 · boc1 PDF page 43

question:
One of the advantages of performing antibody screening (detection) studies using gel
technology is:
options: precise volumes of serum are not required
explanation:
One of the advantages of gel technology containing anti-lgG, as used in antibody
detection testing, is that saline washing is not required.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.3.6] [Harmening 2019, p271]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 160 · boc1 PDF page 43

question: Monoclonal blood banking reagents have which of the following as a disadvantage?
explanation:
Overspecificity can be a disadvantage of monoclonal reagents as all antibodies produced
by the clone recognize only a single epitope. Blending these reagents with other monoclonal
reagents or polyclonal reagents to recognize multiple epitopes has been useful in overcoming
this disadvantage.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.3.5] [Harmening 2019, p106]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 161 · boc1 PDF page 43

question:
The direct antiglobulin test in a suspected case of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
is positive. Which of the following monospecific reagents would be used in further direct
antiglobulin testing?
explanation:
Polyspecific anti-human globulin reagents used to evaluate suspected cases of
autoimmune hemolytic anemia must contain anti-C3d and anti-lgG. Once a positive direct
antiglobulin is noted using a polyspecific reagent, testing with monospecific anti-C3d and
monospecific anti-lgG would be done.
[QCMLS 2021: 1.4.2] [Harmening 2019, p109-110]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 162 · boc1 PDF page 43

question:
Low ionic strength saline (LISS) acts as an enhancement medium and facilitates antibody
uptake by:
explanation:
Low ionic strength saline (LISS) facilitates hemagglutination by decreasing ionic strength
and reducing the zeta potential, allowing for antibodies to react with their respective red cell
antigens. LISS may also increase antibody uptake and reduce incubation times.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.3.4] (Harmening 2019, p69-70]
D. Complement
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 163 · boc1 PDF page 43

question:
The membrane attack complex (MAC) formed during the activation of complement via the
classical pathway consists of:
explanation:
Once activated, the membrane attack complex (MAC) results in cell lysis and includes
C5b through C9.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.4.2.1.1] [Harmening 2019, p60-61]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 164 · boc1 PDF page 44

question:
In ABO hemolytic transfusion reactions, complement is activated via which of the following
pathways?
explanation:
ABO antibodies are very efficient at activating complement via the classical pathway. ABO
antibodies can be potent hemolysins and cause intravascular destruction of incompatible red
cells and acute hemolytic transfusion reactions that can be fatal.
(QCMLS 2021: 1.2.2.1] [Harmening 2019, p59, 119, 378-379]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 165 · boc1 PDF page 44

question:
lgG-sensitized red cells that activate complement may not complete complement activation to
cell lysis. In addition to lgG on the surface of these red cells, what complement component is
present?
explanation:
Some blood group lgG antibodies are only capable of activating the complement cascade
to where C3b is bound to the red cell membrane. Cells of the RES system have receptors for
C3b and sensitized cells may be cleared from the circulation.
[QCMLS 2021 : 1.4.2.1.2] [Harmening 2019, p59-61]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 166 · boc1 PDF page 44

question:
While performing antibody detection studies and compatibility testing, hemolysis is noted
following incubation at 37°C. Which of the following alloantibodies might be present?
explanation:
Anti-PP1 pk is a clinically significant alloantibody found in individuals with the rare p
phenotype. This lgM or lgM and lgG alloantibody is very efficient at complement activation
and often demonstrates hemolysis following incubation at 37°C.
(QCMLS 2021 : 1.3.3] [Harmening 2019, p184]
IV. Physiology and Pathophysiology
A. Physiology of Blood
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 167 · boc1 PDF page 44

question: Which of the following statements is true about hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs)?
options: progenitor cells are capable of self-renewal and limitless proliferation
stem cells make up 95% of total HPCs
stem cells are unable to undergo self-renewal
progenitor cells and stem cells are morphologically unrecognizable
explanation:
Both stem and progenitor cells are unrecognizable morphologically. Stem cells make
up only 0.5% of HPCs, while progenitor cells are close to 3%. Stem cells can undergo
self-renewal while progenitor cells cannot.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 168 · boc1 PDF page 44

question: Key cytokines involved in the differentiation and proliferation of erythrocytes include:
options: erythropoietin (EPO) and granulocyte macrophage-colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF)
granulocyte macrophage-colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and flt3 ligand (FL)
explanation:
EPO and GM-CSF are factors that regulate differentiation and proliferation of
erythrocytes. Different I Ls are involved in regulating production and maturation of HPCs and
leukocytes, including granulocytes, eosinophils, basophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes and
megakaryocyte development. Flt ligands help regulate HPCs, Band T lymphocytes and stem
cells.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 169 · boc1 PDF page 44

question: What hematopoiesis site in adults produces erythrocytes and all of the leukocytes?
explanation:
The bone marrow is the hematopoietic site for erythrocytes and all leukocytes beginning
in the 6th month of gestation and continuing through the adult years. The liver functions as the
site of hematopoiesis during the 3rd month of gestation and the spleen, during 3-6 months of
fetal life. The thymus is involved in the development of T-cells.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 1 · Question 170 · boc1 PDF page 44

question: What differentiates erythrocytes from leukocytes as they develop into mature cells?
options: nuclear chromatin is clumped and condensed
nucleus is removed from the cell
explanation:
Erythrocytes and leukocytes have similar maturation characteristics. These cells develop
condensed, clumped chromatin; the nucleoli disappear; and the cell size decreases with
maturation. The erythrocyte is the only one to lose its nucleus. The leukocyte nucleus is very
visible in mature cells.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.1.3, 4.1.4]
