explanation:
The photomicrograph shows the presence of several red blood cells. RBCs appear
as small (6-8 µm), anucleated, biconcave discs that show a central pallor when the fine
adjustment knob of the microscope is used to slightly adjust the plane being viewed. RBCs
can be confused microscopically with several other urinary constituents such as yeast,
small crystals, and fat globules as well as confounding artifacts such as air bubbles and oil
droplets. Care should be taken to correlate the results of the chemical examination with the
microscopic observations, as RBCs should produce a positive result on the occult blood pad
of the reagent test strip.
[QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.4.1) [Strasinger 2021, p178]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 91 · boc1 PDF page 233

question: Urinary casts are primarily composed of:
explanation:
Casts are primarily composed of uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall proteins), but may also
contain other proteins, such as albumin and immunoglobins. Uromodulin is continuously
excreted by the renal tubular cells, but appears to be increased following exercise and
stressful conditions. In conditions that promote urinary stasis, decreased urinary pH, and/or
the presence of calcium or sodium, uromodulin aggregates into fibrils that mesh to form the
matrix of casts.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.5) [Strasinger 2021, p190]
- ~ - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 92 · boc1 PDF page 233

question: Examination for casts should be performed:
options: after adding glacial acetic acid to the sediment
under high dry power (40x obj.) with bright light
after adding Sternheimer-Malbin stain to the supernatant
using subdued lighting and low power (10x obj.) magnification
explanation:
Casts are much larger than other urinary constituents so they are observed using the
low power (1 Ox) objective and are often found along the edges of the coverslip. Given their
relatively low refractive index, casts may not be visible under bright light. Subdued lighting
should be used which can be accomplished by adjusting the settings of the condenser, iris,
and/or rheostat. If casts are observed at low power, they should be evaluated using high dry
power (40x) to determine the presence of inclusions (eg. WBC, RBC, bacteria) which is used
to further classify the type of cast (eg, WBC cast).
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.2, 3.1.4.5] [Strasinger 2021, p190]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 93 · boc1 PDF page 233

question:
Which of the following casts is most likely to be found in a urine sample from an apparently
healthy person?
explanation:
Hyaline casts are formed in the lumen of the renal tubules and are almost entirely
composed of uromodulin. The presence of 0-2 hyaline casts/LPF is considered normal
and may be present following strenuous exercise, heat exposure, dehydration, or stress in
otherwise healthy adults.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.5.1] [Strasinger 2021, p192]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 94 · boc1 PDF page 233

question: Which of the following casts is most indicative of renal failure/end stage renal disease?
explanation:
Waxy casts are associated with significant urinary stasis as seen in chronic renal failure
and are believed to be caused by degeneration of other casts (eg, hyaline, cellular, granular).
Prolonged/significant urinary stasis allows casts to form in the renal tubules and/or collecting
ducts, which may then be dislodged and viewed in the urinary sediment.
[QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.5.7] [Strasinger 2021, p198]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 95 · boc1 PDF page 234

question:
Shortly after collection of a random urine sample, the laboratorian performed a microscopic
urinalysis and reported the results shown in the table:
test
result
WBC
10-13/HPF
RBC
2-6/HPF
hyaline casts
5-7/LPF
bacteria
1+
The urine sediment is reevaluated by a trainee 2 hours later and similar values were reported
for the WBC, RBC, and bacteria, but they found no hyaline casts. The most probable
explanation for this discrepancy is that the casts dissolved due to a(n):
explanation:
Urine samples should be tested within 1-2 hours of collection to minimize changes
that occur to the chemical and cellular composition of the sample. Samples that contain
urease-producing bacteria will demonstrate an increase in pH over time as urea is converted
into ammonia. This results in an alkaline urine which promotes the dissolution of urinary casts.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.1] [Strasinger 2021, p190]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 96 · boc1 PDF page 234

question:
Which of the following aids in differentiating a spherical transitional cell from a round renal
tubular cell?
options: round renal tubular cells are larger
renal tubular cell nuclei are eccentric
spherical transitional cell nuclei are eccentric
explanation:
Transitional epithelial (urothelial) cells are 20-30 µm and appear in several forms,
including spherical, polyhedral, and caudate, but all forms have centrally-located nuclei. Renal
epithelial cells vary in size (14-60 µm) and shape (columnar, round, oval, cuboidal) depending
on where they originate in the renal tubules, but all typically have eccentric nuclei.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.3.2, 3.1.4.3.3) [Strasinger 2021, p183-184]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 97 · boc1 PDF page 234

question:
The presence of which of the following urine microscopic constituents would best differentiate
between cystitis and pyelonephritis?
explanation:
Cystitis refers to an infection or inflammation of the bladder (eg, lower urinary tract
infection); whereas, pyelonephritis is an infection or inflammation of the renal tubules (eg,
upper urinary tract infection). White blood cells, red blood cells, and bacteria are common
findings of both lower and upper urinary tract infections. The presence of WBC casts would
indicate involvement of the renal tubules and aid in differentiating cystitis from pyelonephritis.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.5.4) [Strasinger 2021, p194]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 98 · boc1 PDF page 234

question: Renal tubular epithelial cell casts are most indicative of:
explanation:
Renal tubular epithelial cells line the proximal and distal convoluted tubules as well as
the collecting ducts of the nephron. Damage to the renal tubules, as may occur in tubular
necrosis, can cause these cells to be dislodged. The cells may then be trapped in casts
forming within the tubules, resulting in the formation of renal tubular epithelial casts.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.5.5] [Strasinger 2021, p195]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 99 · boc1 PDF page 234

question:
Hyaline casts found in the urine of a football player admitted to the hospital following a
concussion are most likely the result of:
explanation:
The formation of hyaline casts is common following strenuous exercise, periods of
dehydration, and situations in which decreased urinary flow occurs.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.5] [Strasinger 2021, p192]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 100 · boc1 PDF page 234

question: Which of the following casts most frequently appears to have broken or serrated edges?
explanation:
Waxy casts are believed to be the result of degeneration of other types of casts (eg,
hyaline, cellular, granular) and are associated with extreme urinary stasis. Due to their
extended time in the renal tubules, they are brittle and often contain notches, cracks, and
jagged edges as the result of disintegration.
[QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.5.7] [Strasinger 2021, p197]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 101 · boc1 PDF page 234

question: To distinguish between a clump of WBCs and a WBC cast, it is important to observe:
options: the presence of a cast matrix
explanation:
White blood cells frequently occur in clumps and can resemble a WBC cast. WBC casts
indicate a more serious tubular infection, whereas WBC clumps can be seen in cystitis so it
is important to properly differentiate them. To positively identify the structure as a WBC cast
rather than a clump of cells, the laboratorian must determine that a cast matrix is present.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.5.4) [Strasinger 2021, p194]
- - - - - ' - - - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 102 · boc1 PDF page 235

question: Renal tubular epithelial cells are most likely to be confused with:
explanation:
Renal tubular epithelial cells vary in size (14-60 µm) and shape (columnar, round, oval,
cuboidal), depending on where they originate in the renal tubules, and have eccentric nuclei.
Given their similar size (10-12 µm), presence of a nucleus, and ratio of nucleus to cytoplasm
content, white blood cells and round renal tubular epithelial cells can be challenging to
differentiate. However, renal tubular epithelial cells are generally slightly larger than WBCs
and their nuclei are eccentric, which may aid in differentiating these cell types. A positive
leukocyte esterase result would also correlate with the presence of WBCs but does not rule
out the presence of renal epithelial cells as both cell types may be present in the sample.
(QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.3.3, 3.1.4.4.2] [Slrasinger 2021, p182)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 103 · boc1 PDF page 235

question: Prior to reporting a red blood cell cast, it is important to observe:
explanation:
RBC casts indicate serious glomerular disease so it is important to properly differentiate
them from other types of casts. To positively identify an RBC cast, the laboratorian must also
observe free-floating RBCs in the sediment and correlate the results with a positive occult
blood value from the chemical examination.
(QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.5.2] [Strasinger 2021, p193)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 104 · boc1 PDF page 235

question: The crystals seen in the photomicrograph may indicate the patient has:
explanation:
The photomicrograph shows the presence of cystine crystals, which appear as colorless,
hexagonal plates in acidic urines. Cystine crystals are associated with cystinuria, which is a
metabolic disorder that prevents reabsorption of cystine in the renal tubules.
(QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.7.4] [Strasinger 2021, p206]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 105 · boc1 PDF page 235

question: The presence of red blood cell casts correlates best with which of the following conditions?
explanation:
RBCs normally should not be able to pass through the glomerular membrane.
The presence of RBC casts indicates there is bleeding within the nephron, or that damage
has occurred to the glomeruli and RBCs are entering the nephron inappropriately, as seen in
glomerulonephritis.
(QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.5.2] [Slrasinger 2021, p192)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 106 · boc1 PDF page 235

question: A white precipitate in a refrigerated urine specimen with pH of 7.5 would most likely be:
explanation:
As the temperature of a urine sample decreases, solutes are more likely to precipitate and
form crystals. After refrigeration of an alkaline urine, amorphous phosphates may precipitate,
leading to the appearance of a white precipitate that does not dissolve upon warming.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.7.3] [Strasinger 2021, p199, 204)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 107 · boc1 PDF page 235

question: Which of the following is an abnormal crystal described as a hexagonal plate?
explanation:
Cystine crystals appear as colorless, hexagonal plates that frequently occur in clumps,
leading to a layered or laminated appearance.
(QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.7.4) [Strasinger 2021, p206]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 108 · boc1 PDF page 235

question: The primary component of most renal calculi is:
explanation:
Approximately 75% of renal calculi are composed of calcium compounds such as calcium
oxalate and calcium phosphate. Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite), uric acid, and
cystine account for a large portion of the remaining 25% of renal calculi.
[QCMLS 2021 : 2.7.5.3] [Strasinger 2021 , p229]

question:
A clear, yellow urine is stored at 5°C as testing will be delayed. When removed from the
refrigerator, the sample appears cloudy. This is most likely due to the presence of:
explanation:
Solutes are more likely to precipitate and form crystals as the temperature of the solution
decreases. After refrigeration, amorphous crystals, such as amorphous urates or amorphous
phosphates, may precipitate and cause the sample to become cloudy. Amorphous urates
will dissolve when the specimen is briefly warmed. Amorphous phosphates can be dissolved
by the addition of acetic acid, but the acid will destroy other sediment constituents, such as
RBCs, and should only be performed after viewing the sample for these other elements.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.6.3, 3.1.4.7.3] [Strasinger 2021, p199]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 110 · boc1 PDF page 236

question: Identify the crystals in the photomicrograph:
explanation:
The photomicrograph shows the presence of cholesterol crystals. Cholesterol crystals
appear in acidic or neutral urines as colorless, rectangular plates with notched corners.
They frequently occur in clumps, leading to a layered or laminated appearance.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4. 7 .5] [Strasinger 2021, p206]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 111 · boc1 PDF page 236

question: Which of the following crystals may be found in an acidic urine?
explanation:
Calcium oxalate crystals are most commonly found in acidic or neutral urines. Ammonium
biurate, calcium phosphate, and triple phosphate are seen in alkaline urines.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.6.1] [Strasinger 2021, p202]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 112 · boc1 PDF page 236

question: Using polarized light microscopy, which of the following urinary elements is birefringent?
explanation:
Cholesterol is capable of polarizing light and demonstrates weak birefringence when
viewed using a polarizing microscope.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.7.5] [Strasinger 2021, p206)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 113 · boc1 PDF page 236

question: Which of the following crystals appear as colorless, fine, silky needles?
explanation:
Tyrosine crystals are colorless or yellow, fine needles that often appear in clusters or
sheaves. They are associated with liver disease and inherited amino acid metabolic disorders
such as tyrosinemia.
[QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.7.7] [Strasinger 2021, p207]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 114 · boc1 PDF page 236

question:
Which of the following crystals would most likely be present in an amber-colored urine yielding
a positive bilirubin?
explanation:
An amber-colored urine is associated with the presence of bilirubin, which is confirmed by
the reaction on the reagent test strip. The presence of bilirubin in the urine sample suggests
liver disease or damage. Tyrosine crystals and leucine crystals may be seen in patients with
liver disease due to impaired amino acid metabolism.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.2.1, 3.1.4.7.7] [Strasinger 2021, p127, 207)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 115 · boc1 PDF page 236

question:
Following ingestion of ethylene glycol (antifreeze), which of the following crystals may be
found in the urine?
explanation:
Following ingestion of ethylene glycol/antifreeze, calcium oxalate crystals in their
monohydrate form may be seen in acidic urines. Unlike the more commonly seen
envelope-shaped dihydrate crystals, monohydrate calcium oxalate crystals appear
as colorless ovals or dumbbells.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.6.1] [Strasinger 2021, p203-204]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 116 · boc1 PDF page 237

question: Cholesterol crystals will most likely be observed in urine with a:
explanation:
The presence of cholesterol crystals in urine is associated with lipiduria which occurs in
nephrotic syndrome. In nephrotic syndrome, >3.5 g of protein are excreted per day in the
urine, which would yield a positive result for the protein pad when tested using a reagent test
strip.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.7.5] [Strasinger 2021 , p206)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 117 · boc1 PDF page 237

question:
The finding of a large amount of uric acid crystals in a urine specimen from a 6-month-old
baby may indicate:
explanation:
The presence of a large amount of uric acid crystals is associated with increased
metabolism of purines and nucleic acids as seen in patients with gout, Lesch-Nyhan
syndrome, or those receiving chemotherapy.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.6.2] [Strasinger 2021, p202, 247]

The photomicrograph shows the presence of a triple phosphate crystal. Triple phosphate

question: Identify the crystals in the photomicrograph:
explanation:
The photomicrograph shows the presence of several uric acid crystals. Uric acid crystals
appear in acidic urines as colorless or yellow-brown rhombic plates. They often appear in
clusters referred to as "rosettes." They may be considered as a normal urinary crystal in small
amounts, but large amounts are associated with increased purine metabolism and would be
considered clinically significant.
[QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.6.2] [Strasinger 2021, p202]

diluting the urine sediment with normal saline
adding a few drops of acetic acid to the sediment

The photomicrograph shows the presence of a large amount of amorphous crystals,
which may inhibit visualization of other clinically significant elements. The crystals are likely
amorphous phosphates because the sample has an alkaline pH. Amorphous phosphates
appear as a white precipitant following centrifugation. They can be dissolved by adding a few
drops of dilute acetic acid to the prepared sediment. This may allow visualization of other
formed elements previously obscured by the crystals; however, the acid will also destroy other
sediment constituents, such as RBCs, and should only be performed after viewing the sample
for these other elements.

question: Polarized light might be used to differentiate between:
options: red blood cells and white blood cells
explanation:
Uric acid crystals most commonly appear as rhombic plates but can also have a 6-sided
shape similar to cystine. Polarizing microscopy can be used to distinguish these 2 types of
crystals as uric acid crystals are strongly birefringent, whereas cystine crystals generally do
not polarize light.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.6.2, 3.1.4.7.4] [Strasinger2021 , p202, 206]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 122 · boc1 PDF page 238

question:
Which of the following contaminants has a dimpled center and can appear as a Maltese cross
under polarized light?
explanation:
Starch granules appear as spheres with a dimpled center and produce a Maltese cross
under polarized light.
[Strasinger 2021, p210]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 123 · boc1 PDF page 238

question:
Which of the following crystals appear as colorless, rhombic plates or rosettes when present
in a urine sample?
explanation:
Uric acid crystals most commonly appear in acidic urines as colorless or yellow-brown
rhombic plates and often appear in clusters referred to as "rosettes." They can also appear as
wedges and 4- or 6-sided plates that can be confused with cystine crystals.
[QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.6.2] [Strasinger 2021, p202]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 124 · boc1 PDF page 239

question: Identify the microscopic element indicated by the arrow in the photomicrograph:
explanation:
The photomicrograph shows a cloth fiber, which is a contaminant in the urine sediment.
Hair and cloth fibers are often mistaken for casts and care must be taken to differentiate them.
Fibers are generally longer, more retractile, and will polarize light.
[Strasinger 2021, p210]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 125 · boc1 PDF page 239

question:
A newer laboratorian is having trouble differentiating between red blood cells, oil droplets, and
yeast during microscopic analysis of urine sediments. To aid in differentiation, they add a few
drops of glacial acetic acid to the sediment which will:
explanation:
The addition of a few drops of glacial acetic acid would cause RBCs to lyse, but would
not affect oil droplets and yeast. Care must be taken as the addition of the acid would also
lyse other formed elements and should only be added to an aliquot of the urine sediment after
evaluation of the other elements.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.4.1] (Strasinger 2021, p179]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 126 · boc1 PDF page 239

question:
When identifying urinary crystals, which of the following reagent test strip results would be
most helpful?
explanation:
Precipitation of urinary crystals is influenced by several factors including: concentration
of urine solutes (eg, calcium, uric acid), temperature, and the pH of the solution.
When differentiating crystals with a similar appearance, knowing the pH of the sample may be
of value as some crystals are more soluble in an acidic pH and will only precipitate in alkaline
urines (eg, triple phosphate), while others are more soluble in an alkaline pH and precipitate
in acidic urines (eg, uric acid).
(QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.6, 3.1.4.7] [Strasinger2021, p199]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 127 · boc1 PDF page 239

question: Bacteria are considered significant in the urine sediment when the:
explanation:
The bladder is normally a sterile environment and bacteria should not be present in the
urine. Samples collected by catheterization and suprapubic aspiration are considered sterile,
but other methods (eg, random, clean-catch, pediatric U-bag) are prone to contamination
with bacteria from the skin and/or genital region. If testing is delayed, bacteria will continue
to multiply in the sample and can generate a falsely positive nitrite. The presence of WBCs in
the sample confirm the bacteria are present due to an active infection.
[QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.4.2, 3.1.4.8.2, 3.1.5.6] [Strasinger 2021, p187]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 128 · boc1 PDF page 239

question: Which of the following must exhibit rapid motility in order to be identified in a urine sediment?
explanation:
Trichomonas vagina/is is a pear- or turnip-shaped flagellate primarily associated with
vaginal infections. It has four anterior flagella and an undulating membrane, but may be
mistaken for a WBC or renal tubular epithelial cell in urine samples. To differentiate these
elements, the laboratorian should look for motility, which indicates the element is a flagellate.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.8.3] [Strasinger 2021, p189]

The photomicrograph shows the presence of numerous rod-shaped bacteria (bacilli).
Many of the bacteria that cause urinary tract infections convert nitrates into nitrites. Given
sufficient incubation time in the bladder, these bacteria will convert the nitrates in the urine
into nitrites, which will generate a positive reaction on the nitrite test pad of the reagent test

(QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.8.2, 3.1.3.10) [Strasinger2021, p158, 187]

question:
The sediment of a urine specimen with a reagent strip glucose of 250 mg/dl (13.8 mmol/L),
pH of 5.5, and negative nitrite shows the presence of small, ovoid cells that are budding.
These results are most consistent with a urinary tract infection by:
explanation:
Yeast appear as small, colorless ovoid cells similar to RBCs. The cells show budding that
aids in identifying them as yeast, of which Candida albicans is a frequent cause of urinary
tract infections. The ideal conditions for growth of Candida albicans include an acidic pH and
the presence of glucose, which explains why patients with diabetes frequently have urinary
tract infections caused by Candida.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.8.1) [Strasinger 2021, p189)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 132 · boc1 PDF page 240

question:
Which of the following urinary crystals appear as yellow-brown spheres with concentric circles
when viewed microscopically?
explanation:
Leucine crystals appear in acidic or neutral urines as yellow-brown spheres with
concentric circles and radial striations. Their presence is associated with liver disease and
inborn errors of metabolism (eg, MSUD).
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.7.8] [Strasinger 2021, p208)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 133 · boc1 PDF page 240

question: Identify the elements in the photomicrograph:
options:
white blood cells
d renal tubular epithelial cells
explanation:
The photomicrograph shows the presence of budding yeast. Yeast appear as small,
colorless ovoid cells that are highly retractile. The presence of budding and branching aids in
differentiating yeast cells from RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.8.1] [Strasinger 2021, p188]

question: The normal renal threshold for glucose in an adult is approximately:
explanation:
After formation of the plasma ultrafiltrate by the glomerulus, substances are reabsorbed
and secreted in the renal tubules. Tubular reabsorption occurs through active and passive
transport mechanisms. Normally, substances are actively transported from the ultrafiltrate
into the blood stream until the renal threshold is met. The renal threshold is the plasma
concentration at which a substance, such as glucose, is no longer reabsorbed by the
proximal convoluted tubules. The renal threshold for glucose ranges from 160-180 mg/dl
(8.88-9.99 mmol/L).
(QCMLS 2021: 2.7.2.5) [Strasinger 2021, p110, 148]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 135 · boc1 PDF page 241

question:
If the total volume of urine excreted in a 24-hour period by an adult patient is 300 ml, their
condition would be termed:
explanation:
The volume of urine excreted per day is dependent on several factors, such as hydration
status, renal function, hormonal control, and the use of diuretics. Healthy adults produce
1-2 L (1000-2000 ml) of urine per day. The prefix o/igo- means scanty and oliguria refers
to production of less than 400 ml/day. The prefix an- means not with anuria referring to
cessation of urinary flow. Poly- means many and the term polyuria is used to describe the
production of more than 2.5-3.0 Lin a 24-hour period. Patients with urinary tract infections
often experience pain during urination, which is termed dysuria (dys- means bad or ill).
[Strasinger 2021, p93]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 136 · boc1 PDF page 241

question: The normal glomerular filtration rate is:
explanation:
Plasma is filtered at the glomerulus at a rate of 120 ml/min forming the plasma
ultrafiltrate. The rate of glomerular filtration can be evaluated using a clearance test in which
the concentration of an analyte is measured in both a urine sample and a paired blood
sample.
(QCMLS 2021: 2.7.2.2) [Strasinger 2021, p106, 115)

source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 137 · boc1 PDF page 241

question:
A urine sediment from a 52-year-old patient is shown in the photomicrograph:
The elements seen in the sediment may indicate the patient has:
explanation:
The photomicrograph shows the presence of uric acid crystals. Uric acid crystals
appear in acidic urines as colorless or yellow-brown rhombic plates and are associated with
increased metabolism of purines and nucleic acids, as seen in patients with gout.
(QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.4.6.2) [Strasinger 2021, p202]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 138 · boc1 PDF page 242

question:
A physician wants to determine if an abdominal fluid collected during surgery is urine. Which
of the following analytes would normally be present in the urine of an apparently healthy
patient?
explanation:
Creatinine is a waste product excreted via the kidneys. As such, urine normally contains
a high concentation of creatinine, making it a useful measurement in determining if a fluid is
urine. Normally, urine should be negative for protein, glucose, and bilirubin using a reagent
test strip.
(QCMLS 2021: 2.7.3.1, 2.7.3.2) [Strasinger 2021, p93, 143, 148, 154)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 139 · boc1 PDF page 242

question: Arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone [ADH]) regulates the reabsorption of:
explanation:
Arginine vasopressin (AVP), also known as antidiuretic hormone (ADH), is produced
in the hypothalamus and secreted by the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolality and
sodium concentrations are elevated. AVP regulates the permeability of the walls of the distal
convoluted tubule and the collecting ducts to water. When the body is dehydrated (elevated
plasma osmolality/increased sodium), AVP is released by the pituitary gland to increase the
permeability of the walls and allow water to be reabsorbed into the bloodstream.
(QCMLS 2021: 2.7.2.3] [Strasinger 2021, p110]

question:
Which of the following components would be present in the filtrate as a result of glomerular
damage?
explanation:
Plasma is filtered at the glomerulus forming a plasma ultrafiltrate. When the glomerular
membrane is intact, only substances with a molecular weight <70,000 (eg, urea, glucose,
amino acids) will pass through. Larger molecular weight substances and cells (eg, RBCs)
cannot readily pass through the glomerular membrane and their presence in urine is
associated with damage to the glomerulus.
[QCMLS 2021: 2.7.2.2] [Strasinger 2021 , p106]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 141 · boc1 PDF page 242

question: Polyuria is often associated with:
explanation:
Patients with diabetes mellitus often have elevated plasma glucose concentrations
resulting in glucosuria. Glucose is an osmotically active substance that results in excretion of
urine volumes >2.5-3.0 L per 24 hours (polyuria).
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.5.2] (Strasinger 2021, p93]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 142 · boc1 PDF page 242

question: Cessation of urine flow is termed:
explanation:
Healthy adults produce 1-2 L (1000-2000 ml) of urine per day, but the total volume is
dependent on several factors such as hydration status, renal function, hormonal control, and
the use of diuretics. The prefix an- means not, or without, and anuria refers to cessation of
urinary flow.
[Strasinger 2021, p93]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 143 · boc1 PDF page 242

question: Ketonuria is associated with increased metabolism of:
explanation:
Acetoacetic acid, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone, collectively referred to as ketones,
are intermediate products of lipid (fat) metabolism. When carbohydrates cannot be used to
generate energy, fats are used as an alternative energy source and ketones can be detected
in the urine.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.3.5] [Strasinger 2021 , p151]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 144 · boc1 PDF page 243

question: Bilirubinuria may be associated with:
explanation:
Bilirubin is a product of hemoglobin degradation. Conjugated bilirubin is normally
transported to the intestines, where it is converted into urobilinogen by intestinal normal flora
and excreted in the feces. A biliary tract obstruction may inhibit the normal flow of conjugated
bilirubin into the intestine causing it to enter the bloodstream. Conjugated bilirubin is watersoluble and will be filtered into the urine, leading to a positive bilirubin result on the reagent
test strip.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.3.8, 3.1.5.5] [Strasinger2021, p154)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 145 · boc1 PDF page 243

question:
Hepatic disorders may result in the presence of which of the following types of urinary
crystals?
explanation:
Patients with hepatic disease or damage may leak conjugated bilirubin into the
bloodstream, where it can be filtered and excreted via the kidneys. In acidic urines, bilirubin
crystals appear as small clusters of fine, yellow-brown needles and are considered clinically
significant.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.1.4.7.6, 3.1.5.5] [Strasinger 2021, p208]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 146 · boc1 PDF page 243

question: A patient with renal tubular acidosis would most likely excrete a urine with a:
explanation:
There are several forms of renal tubular acidosis (RTA), which is characterized by
decreased ability to secrete hydrogen ions in the distal convoluted tubules (distal RTA) and/or
decreased ability to reabsorb bicarbonate in the proximal convoluted tubules (proximal RTA).
This leads to excretion of an alkaline urine despite the patient being in a state of metabolic
acidosis.
[QCMLS 2021 : 2.7.5.2.2] [Brunzel 2018, p220]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 147 · boc1 PDF page 243

question: Glycosuria may be due to:
explanation:
Glucose is filtered at the glomerulus and reabsorbed by active transport mechanisms in
the proximal convoluted tubules (PCT) up to the renal threshold. Damage and/or dysfunction
of the PCT may cause decreased glucose reabsorption leading to inappropriate excretion of
glucose in the urine (glycosuria) and a normal or low plasma glucose concentration.
(QCMLS 2021: 2.7.2.3, 3.1.5.3] [Strasinger 2021, p110, 226]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 148 · boc1 PDF page 243

question: The area of the nephron that is impermeable to water is the:
explanation:
Following significant reabsorption of water and solutes in the proximal convoluted
tubule, the filtrate enters the descending limb of the loop of Henle. In this section of the renal
tubules, water is passively reabsorbed due to the high osmotic gradient of the renal medulla,
effectively concentrating the filtrate. To prevent excessive absorption of water, the walls of the
ascending limb of the loop of Henle are impermeable to water.
[QCMLS 2021: 2.7.2.3] [Strasinger 2021 , p110]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 149 · boc1 PDF page 243

question: The urinary tract structures primarily responsible for renal concentration are the:
explanation:
The juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops of Henle that allow the urinary filtrate to
pass through the renal medulla; whereas cortical nephrons, located in the renal cortex, have
short loops of Henle that do not reach the medulla. The renal medulla has a high osmotic
gradient that promotes passive reabsorption of water in the descending loop of Henle leading
to concentration of the filtrate.
(QCMLS 2021: 2.7.1.1) [Strasinger 2021 , p106]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 3 · Question 150 · boc1 PDF page 243

explanation:
Urine samples with a red appearance may contain RBCs, hemoglobin, myoglobin,
or porphyrins. The red coloration may also be the result of certain drugs and/or foods.
The positive occult blood reaction indicates the sample contains RBCs, hemoglobin, or
myoglobin. Upon microscopic examination, presence of only a few RBCs suggests the

The most common causes of ATN are renal ischemia and exposure to nephrotoxins such as
hemoglobin and myoglobin.

question: Failure of the nephron to produce ammonia from glutamine will result in urine with a:
explanation:
Ammonia is produced in the renal tubules from the amino acid glutamine. The ammonia
reacts with a hydrogen ion in the filtrate forming an ammonium ion, which is excreted in the
urine. Failure of the nephron to produce ammonia allows the hydrogen ions in the filtrate to be
reabsorbed leading to metabolic acidosis and a high urinary pH (alkaline).
[QCMLS 2021: 2.8.3] [Strasinger 2021, p111]
E. Disease States

question: A random urine sample with an increased microalbumin concentration is predictive of:
explanation:
Patients with hypertension and diabetes mellitus are at risk for developing kidney
disease (nephropathy). The presence of small amounts of albumin in the urine, termed
microalbuminuria, is used to detect early development of kidney disease.
[QCMLS 2021 : 3.1.3.6] [Strasinger 2021, p145]

question:
Acetylcholinesterase activity may be measured on amniotic fluid when a positive
alpha-fetoprotein result is obtained to evaluate for:
explanation:
Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is an enzyme found in the central nervous system, RBCs,
skeletal muscle tissue, and fetal serum. When analyses of maternal serum and amniotic fluid
yield elevated AFP results, the amniotic fluid should be tested to determine the AChE activity,
as it is a more specific indicator for neural tube disorders.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.2.6.5] [Strasinger 2021, p332]

question: A mildly increased CSF lactate (25-30 mg/dL) is generally associated with:
explanation:
CSF lactate concentrations are increased in meningitis and conditions that cause
hypoxia in the CNS. Fungal and tubercular meningitis are associated with mildly increased
lactate concentrations (>25 mg/dl) and and bacterial meningitis yields significantly elevated
(>35 mg/dl) lactate concentrations.
(QCMLS 2021 : 3.3.5.3) [Strasinger 2021, p268]

question:
A decreased CSF total protein concentration may indicate the occurrence of which of the
following?
explanation:
Elevated CSF total protein concentrations may be associated with meningitis, cerebral
hemorrhage, and neurologic diseases, such as MS, due to inappropriate passage of proteins
through the blood-brain barrier or increased intrathecal production of immunoglobulins.
A decreased total protein may be the result of CSF leakage, recent lumbar puncture, or
dilution caused by rapid CSF production.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.3.5.2] [Strasinger 2021, p266]

question: An acholic or pale/clay-colored stool is characteristic of:
explanation:
Feces is normally orange-brown due to the presence of bile pigments produced from
bilirubin in the liver and intestines. In conditions where the biliary duct is partially or completely
obstructed, bile pigments are not present and the stool has a pale or clay-colored appearance
termed "acholic."
[QCMLS 2021: 3.7.3.1] [Strasinger 2021, p343]

question:
A vaginal swab is received in the laboratory for testing and immediately placed in sterile
physiological saline to prepare a suspension. A wet mount is prepared and the laboratorian
reports the presence of numerous clue cells. This most likely indicates the patient has:
explanation:
Clue cells are squamous epithelial cells with at least 75% of their surface covered by
coccobacilli. This makes the cell appear granular with an irregular border described as
"shaggy." Their presence in vaginal secretions indicates bacterial vaginosis caused by
Gardnerella vagina/is.

are neutrophils. These results may indicate the patient has:
explanation:
WBC are not normally present in feces. The presence of neutrophils suggests of an
inflammatory condition in which the mucosal wall has been compromised, whereas the
presence of lymphocytes is associated with noninflammatory conditions.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.7.5.2] [Strasinger 2021, p343]

question: The presence of rice bodies in a synovial fluid is strongly associated with:
explanation:
Rice bodies are white, free-floating particles that appear in synovial fluid. They are pieces
of cartilage covered by fibrinous tissue that resemble polished, shiny grains of rice that vary in
size. They may be seen in many arthritic conditions, but they are most commonly observed in
association with rheumatoid arthritis.
[QCMLS 2021: 3.5.4.2] [Brunzel 2018, p277]

question: A stool specimen that appears black and tarlike should be tested for the presence of:
explanation:
Feces normally has an orange-brown color. Samples that appear black or tar-like,
referred to as "melena," are associated with the presence of blood originating from
the upper gastrointestinal tract, but may also be the result of medications or therapies
(eg, coal ingestion). An occult blood test may be performed to evaluate if the sample
contains blood.
[QCMLS 2021 : 3.7.3.1, 3.7.4.1] [Strasinger 2021, p343, 345]

question: Peripheral blood smears from patients with untreated pernicious anemia are characterized by:
explanation:
The impaired DNA synthesis associated with pernicious anemia causes decreased
production of all blood cells as well as abnormally large, macrocytic RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.2.1, 14.6]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 52 · boc1 PDF page 291

question:
Laboratory tests performed on a patient indicate macrocytosis and pancytopenia. Which of
the following disorders is most likely?
explanation:
The impaired DNA synthesis associated with a vitamin B12 deficiency causes decreased
production of all blood cells as well as abnormally large, macrocytic RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 53 · boc1 PDF page 291

question: The characteristic morphologic feature in folic acid deficiency Is:
explanation:
In folate deficiency (megaloblastic anemia), the peripheral blood smear will
characteristically show abnormally large RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.2.1, 14.6]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 55 · boc1 PDF page 292

question:
Megaloblastic asynchronous development in the bone marrow indicates which one of the
following?
explanation:
Megaloblastic anemia is caused by impaired DNA synthesis and results in asynchronous
development of blood cells in the bone marrow.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.2.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 57 · boc1 PDF page 292

question: Which of the following are found in association with megaloblastic anemia?
explanation:
Megaloblastic anemias result in pancytopenia, which includes neutropenia and
thrombocytopenia.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.2.1, 14.6)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 58 · boc1 PDF page 292

question:

In anemia of chronic inflammation, iron is present, but it is trapped in macrophages and
unavailable to developing RBCs. Therefore, iron levels can be decreased, but the ability to
bind iron (TIBC) will also be decreased. Transferrin saturation may also be low or normal.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.2.1, 14.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 59 · boc1 PDF page 292

question: A characteristic morphologic feature in hemoglobin C disease is:
explanation:
Peripheral blood cell morphology in HbC disease characteristically includes target cells
and hexagonal or rod-shaped crystals (hemoglobin C crystals).
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.7.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 60 · boc1 PDF page 293

question: Thalassemias are characterized by:
options: structural abnormalities in the hemoglobin molecule
explanation:
Thalassemias are quantitative decreases in the production of globin chains needed for
hemoglobin synthesis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.1.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 61 · boc1 PDF page 293

question: Laboratory findings in hereditary spherocytosis include:
explanation:
The band 3 reduction test (also called the eosin-5-maleimide binding test or EMA) is a
more sensitive procedure for confirming hereditary spherocytosis.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.3.1.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 63 · boc1 PDF page 293

question: Which of the following types of polycythemia is a severely burned patient most likely to have?
explanation:
Burn patients can develop relative polycythemia that results from loss of body fluid and
subsequent dehydration.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.2.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 64 · boc1 PDF page 293

question: The characteristic morphologic feature in lead poisoning is:
explanation:
Basophilic stippling is a classic laboratory finding in lead poisoning.
{QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.1.3)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 65 · boc1 PDF page 293

question: The white cell feature most characteristic of pernicious anemia is:
explanation:
Hypersegmented neutrophils are the most prominent WBC feature associated with
pernicious anemia and megaloblastic anemias in general.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.2.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 66 · boc1 PDF page 293

question: Which parameter is most consistently abnormal in cases of hereditary spherocytosis?
explanation:
RBC indices are helpful in diagnosing hereditary spherocytosis, as the MCV and MCH
are usually normal and the MCHC is increased. Spherocytes are the only erythrocytes with an
elevated MCHC.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.1.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 67 · boc1 PDF page 294

question: What protein is commonly defective in hereditary elliptocytosis?
explanation:
Hereditary elliptocytosis may be linked to defects in several different RBC membrane
proteins including spectrin.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.1.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 68 · boc1 PDF page 294

question: What is the most common mechanism resulting in hereditary stomatocytosis?
options: inability to repair oxidative stress damage
ATP depletion due to glycolytic enzyme deficiency
explanation:
Hereditary stomatocytosis includes a group of disorders in which the RBC membrane
displays abnormalities in cation permeability.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.3.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 69 · boc1 PDF page 294

question: The basic mechanism associated with the development of sideroblastic anemia is:
options: enzymatic defect in heme synthesis causes iron accumulation
quantitative decrease in the production of globin chains
ineffective erythropoietin production decreases RBC response
explanation:
Sideroblastic anemias may be inherited or acquired and caused by either mutations in
heme synthetic enzymes or impaired activity of heme. The enzymatic defects or impaired
activity result in excess iron accumulation in mitochondria and developing RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.1.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 70 · boc1 PDF page 294

question: Individuals with Fanconi anemia characteristically show:
explanation:
Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder showing normocytic anemia.
Physically, patients show short stature, microcephaly and hyperpigmentation. HbF is elevated
and patient survival is limited.
[Ciesla 2017, p109]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 71 · boc1 PDF page 294

question:
Which of the following tumors are associated with erythrocytosis due to excessive
erythropoietin production?
options: squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
explanation:
An inappropriate increase in erythropoietin has been associated with certain tumors that
secrete erythropoietin or an erythropoietin-like substance. Tumors are often associated with
renal disease.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.7.2.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 72 · boc1 PDF page 294

question:
Which of the following features of G6PD deficiency are typically present on a Wright-Giemsa
stained peripheral blood smear?
explanation:
During or immediately following a hemolytic episode related to a G6PD deficiency,
abnormalities in erythrocytes may include poikilocytosis, polychromasia, some spherocytes,
and bite cells. Heinz bodies are only visible with a supravital stain.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 73 · boc1 PDF page 294

question: Which abnormal RBC morphology is associated with pyruvate kinase deficiency?
explanation:
The peripheral blood smear in pyruvate kinase deficiency may show echinocytes and
sometimes irregularly contracted cells.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.3.1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 74 · boc1 PDF page 294

question: Which of the following hemoglobinopathies is associated with rod shaped crystals?
explanation:
In hemoglobin C disease, hexagonal or rod-shaped crystals (hemoglobin C crystals) may
be seen in RBCs, especially in patients who have received a splenectomy.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.7.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 75 · boc1 PDF page 294

question: Which of the following statements about hemoglobins D and G is true?
options: they both migrate with HbS on alkaline gel
they are both caused by mutations in the beta-globin gene
they cannot be separated by solubility testing
explanation:
HbD and HbG are abnormal variants that migrate at the same position as HbS on alkaline
electrophoresis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.6.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 76 · boc1 PDF page 295

question: This hemoglobinopathy results from a fusion product of the delta and beta gene:
explanation:
Hblepore is a variant formed from the fusion of delta and beta genes that occurs from
abnormal crossing-over during meiosis. The resulting fusion gene produces hybrid delta/beta
globin chains that combine with 2 alpha chains to synthesize Hblepore.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.7.10]
-
- - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 77 · boc1 PDF page 295

question: Which of the following is consistent with the diagnosis of heterozygous beta-thalassemia?
explanation:
The RBC count is increased in heterozygous beta thalassemia more than expected for
the hemoglobin concentration.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 78 · boc1 PDF page 295

question:
Hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH) is due to a loss of expression of this globin
chain:
t.1Ls
explanation:
HPFH is caused by either the absence of beta and delta chain synthesis or a loss
of suppression of the gamma globin gene through mutations of proteins inhibiting gene
expression or in the gamma gene promoter region.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.3.7.9]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 79 · boc1 PDF page 295

question: What is the specificity of cold autoagglutinin disease?
explanation:
The antibody produced in cold agglutinin disease is usually an autoantibody with anti-I
specificity.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.3.3)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 80 · boc1 PDF page 295

question: What is the most common presentation of paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria?
explanation:
Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is most often seen in children with viral infections.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.3)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 81 · boc1 PDF page 295

question: Which of the following is the most common cause of anemia in hospitalized patients?
explanation:
Anemia of chronic inflammation (disease) is a common cause of anemia in hospitalized
patients. It is associated with infections and inflammatory or malignant conditions.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.1.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 82 · boc1 PDF page 295

question:
In a patient with an increased red cell mass into the 99th percentile and serum erythropoietin
level below reference range for normal, which of the following criteria confirms a diagnosis of
polycythemia vera?
explanation:
In 95-100% of polycythemia vera patients the JAK2 V617 mutation is present.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.3.1.2, t4.11)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 83 · boc1 PDF page 295

question:
A medical technologist is examining a peripheral smear and notices 7 large segmented
neutrophils with between 5 and 7 lobes. Everything else about the CBC is otherwise normal.
This observed morphologic change might develop months ahead of which of the following
changes:
options: an increase in MCV, MCH, and ROW
a decrease in MCV, MCH, and ROW
an increase in metamyelocytes and bands
explanation:
The MCV and MCH are increased in megaloblastic anemia. Hypersegmented neutrophils
are one of the distinguishing features of megaloblastic anemia. Anisocytosis (elevated ROW)
is also present. Hypersegmented neutrophils may be seen before the megaloblastic anemia is
fully developed.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.2.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 84 · boc1 PDF page 296

question: The red blood cells in this image are representative of an anemia that is:
explanation:
Nonmegaloblastic macrocytic anemias are characterized by erythrocytes that are round
and macrocytic. This is in contrast to megaloblastic anemias in which macro-ovalocytes are
present.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.2.2)
4

source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 85 · boc1 PDF page 296

question: This image of the blood smear from a newborn most likely represents:
explanation:
Spherocytes and polychromasia are diagnostically important findings in RBCs in
hemolytic disease of the newborn due to ABO incompatibility. Nucleated RBCs may also be
seen in the peripheral blood of newborns.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7 .1.3.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 86 · boc1 PDF page 296

question: Hemoglobin H disease results from:
explanation:
HbH disease occurs when 3 of 4 alpha genes are deleted.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1 .1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 87 · boc1 PDF page 296

question: The M:E ratio in polycythemia vera is usually:
explanation:
Granulopoiesis and erythropoiesis are both often increased in polycythemia vera,
resulting in a normal M:E ratio.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.3.1.2, 14.11] (McKenzie 2020, p538] delete QC reference and update McK to McKenzie
2020, p538
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 88 · boc1 PDF page 297

explanation:
Iron deficiency anemia laboratory features include: decreased serum iron, serum ferritin,
percent saturation, bone marrow iron stores and increased TIBC.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.1.1; 14.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 89 · boc1 PDF page 297

question:
A patient has a tumor that concentrates erythropoietin. He is most likely to have which of the
following types of polycythemia?
explanation:
Secondary polycythemia can occur inappropriately when renal tumors secrete
erythropoietin.
[McKenzie 2020, p539]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 90 · boc1 PDF page 297

question: Which of the following types of polycythemia is most often associated with lung disease?
explanation:
Lung disease causes tissue hypoxia and results in secondary polycythemia.
(QCMLS 2021 : 4. 7 .2.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 91 · boc1 PDF page 297

question:
A patient has been treated for a malignant tumor for several years. His blood smear now
shows:
oval macrocytes
Howell-Jolly bodies
hypersegmented neutrophils
large, agranular platelets
The most probable cause of this blood picture is:
explanation:
Some drugs interfere with DNA synthesis and result in megaloblastic anemia. Peripheral
blood findings reflect the megaloblastic process and include characteristic cellular changes
to include oval macrocytes, RBC inclusions, hypersegmented neutrophils, and platelet
abnormalities.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.2.1, 14.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 92 · boc1 PDF page 297

question: How does the bone marrow respond to anemic stress?
options: expand production, rush platelets into circulation
explanation:
When the bone marrow senses anemia, it increases production of red cells in a premature
fashion, releasing nucleated red blood cells. Polychromasia will also be seen on the
peripheral blood smear.
[Ciesla 2017, p27]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 93 · boc1 PDF page 297

question:
Which of the following conditions may contribute to lethargy, abdominal pain, and
hemoglobinuria in some patients with a G6PD deficiency?
explanation:
Favism (consumption of fava beans) is the second most severe clinical condition of
G6PD deficiency. After ingestion of fava beans an individual may experience hemoglobinuria,
lethargy and abdominal pain.
[Ciesla 2017, p107]
B. Leukocytes
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 94 · boc1 PDF page 298

question: The most likely cause of the macrocytosis that often accompanies primary myelofibrosis is:
explanation:
Myelofibrosis is often accompanied by a folate deficiency, which develops because of
increased consumption by the malignant clone and results in macrocytic anemia.
[McKenzie 2020, p542]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 95 · boc1 PDF page 298

question: Giant, vacuolated, multinucleated erythroid precursors are present in which of the following?
explanation:
RBC precursors in erythroleukemia display several dysplastic characteristics.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 96 · boc1 PDF page 298

question: Which of the following is a significant feature of dyserythropoiesis?
explanation:
Megaloblastoid erythropoiesis is a morphologic feature characteristic of dyserythropoiesis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 97 · boc1 PDF page 298

question: The M:E ratio in erythroleukemia is usually:
explanation:
In erythroleukemia, 50% or more of nucleated bone marrow cells are normoblasts, which
indicates a decrease in the myeloid component and results in a low M:E.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.1.1, 14.9]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 98 · boc1 PDF page 298

question: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is often a complication of:
explanation:
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia may be associated with an underlying lymphoproliferative
disease such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.3.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 99 · boc1 PDF page 298

question: Elevation of the total granulocyte count above 7.5 x 103/µL (7.5 x 109/L) is termed:
explanation:
An absolute neutrophilic leukocytosis occurs when the total granulocyte count (circulating
neutrophils) is greater than 7 .5 x 109/L.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 100 · boc1 PDF page 298

question: Elevation of the total white cell count above 11.0 x 103/µL (11 x 109/L) is termed:
explanation:
Leukocytosis occurs when the total leukocyte count is greater than 11.0 x 103/µL.
[McKenzie 2020, p452]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 101 · boc1 PDF page 298

question: Elevation of the lymphocyte percentage above 45% is termed:
explanation:
A relative lymphocytosis is defined as more than 45% lymphocytes on a manual
differential or automated cell count.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.8.3.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 102 · boc1 PDF page 298

question: The Philadelphia chromosome is formed by a translocation between:
explanation:
The Philadelphia chromosome results when chromosomes 22 and 9 are reciprocally
translocated.
[McKenzie 2020, p523]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 103 · boc1 PDF page 299

question: The mechanism causing catecholamine-induced neutrophilia includes:
options: a shift in granulocytes from the marginating pool to the circulating pool
an increased exit of granulocytes from the circulation
a decreased exit of granulocytes from the bone marrow
granulocyte return from the tissues to the circulating pool
explanation:
Catecholamines such as epinephrine cause demargination of neutrophils.
[Rodak 2016, p485]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 104 · boc1 PDF page 299

question: What accounts for the frequent smudge cells in CLL?
explanation:
The malignant cells in CLL are more fragile than normal lymphocytes and disperse during
smear preparation, producing smudge cells.
[McKenzie 2020, p626]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 105 · boc1 PDF page 299

question:
A 14-year-old boy is seen in the ER complaining of a sore throat, swollen glands and fatigue.
The CBC results are:

result
WBC

absolute reactive lymphs

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
In infectious mononucleosis, the leukocyte count is usually increased due to an absolute
lymphocytosis and increase in reactive lymphocytes.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.3.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 106 · boc1 PDF page 299

question: The M:E ratio in chronic myelocytic leukemia is usually:
explanation:
CML is associated with a marked increase in the M:E, reflective of enhanced
myelopoiesis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.3.1.2.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 107 · boc1 PDF page 299

question:
In the World Health Organization (WHO) classification, acute myelomonocytic leukemia would
be named acute myeloid leukemia (AML):
explanation:
Acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AMML) is classified by the WHO in the category
of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), not otherwise specified.This leukemia was previously
classified by the French-America-British cooperative group as FAB M4.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1.1, 14.9]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 108 · boc1 PDF page 299

question: Abnormalities found in erythroleukemia include:
explanation:
Features of acute erythroid leukemia may include dysplastic changes in erythrocytes such
as megaloblastoid development.
[McKenzie 2020, p600]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 109 · boc1 PDF page 300

question: Neutropenia is usually associated with:
explanation:
Neutropenia is a result of many conditions, including viral and overwhelming bacterial
infections. Viral infections typically cause a lymphocytosis and subsequent relative decrease
in neutrophils.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.8.3.1] [McKenzie 2020, p456]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 110 · boc1 PDF page 300

question: Auer rods are most likely present in which of the following?
explanation:
Auer rods are associated with some cases of AML.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 111 · boc1 PDF page 300

question: In an uncomplicated case of infectious mononucleosis, which type of cells is affected?
explanation:
Lymphocytes are the predominant cells responding to a viral infection, such as infectious
mononucleosis.
(QCMLS 2021 : 4.8.3.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 113 · boc1 PDF page 300

question:
The reactive lymphocyte seen in the peripheral blood smear of patients with infectious
mononucleosis is probably derived from which of these cell types?
explanation:
Most reactive lymphocytes in infectious mononucleosis are cytotoxic, CDS positive T cells.
[McKenzie 2020, p477]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 114 · boc1 PDF page 300

question:
The disease most frequently present in patients with reactive lymphocytosis and persistently
negative heterophile antibody tests is:
explanation:
CMV is the most common cause of a heterophile-negative reactive lymphocytosis.
[McKenzie 2020, p480)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 115 · boc1 PDF page 300

question: Dwarf or micromegakaryocytes may be found in the peripheral blood of patients with:
explanation:
Dysplastic platelets, including micromegakaryocytes, may be seen in the peripheral blood
in primary myelofibrosis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.4.1, 14.16] [McKenzie 2020, p543]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 116 · boc1 PDF page 301

question: Which of the following is associated with pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly?
explanation:
Peripheral blood dysplasia, such as pseudo-Pelger-Huet neutrophils, may be seen
in CML.
[McKenzie 2020, p526]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 117 · boc1 PDF page 301

question: Increased numbers of basophils are often seen in:
options: erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn)
explanation:
Basophils may be increased in CML as well as immature neutrophils and eosinophils.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.9.3.1.2, 14.11] [McKenzie 2020, p526]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 118 · boc1 PDF page 301

question: A hypercellular marrow with an M:E ratio of 6:1 is most commonly due to:
explanation:
The myeloid to erythroid ratio (M:E) relates the bone marrow numbers of all granulocytes
and precursors to the numbers of all nucleated RBC precursors. A hypercellular marrow (M:E)
of 6:1 indicates more myeloid than erythroid cells in the bone marrow.
[McKenzie 2020, p961]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 119 · boc1 PDF page 301

Peripheral blood findings in primary myelofibrosis are numerous and include abnormal
RBC morphology, such as teardrop cells. Also note frequently decreased platelets and

[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.3.1.2, 14.11] [McKenzie 2020, p542)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 120 · boc1 PDF page 301

question:
A SO-year-old man is admitted into the hospital with acute leukemia. Laboratory findings
include the results shown in this table:
test

myeloperoxidase stain
blast cells negative

These results are most consistent with:
options: chronic lymphocytic leukemia in lymphoblastic transformation
chronic myelogenous leukemia in lymphoblastic transformation
explanation:
Some cases (30%) of CML in terminal phase (blast crisis) may present as an acute
lymphoblastic leukemia.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.9.3.1.2.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 121 · boc1 PDF page 302

readmitted because of cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory findings are shown in this table:

thrombocytopenia, and a progressive increase in blasts. Blasts may exceed 20% in the
peripheral blood and bone marrow. A positive Philadelphia chromosome and BCRIABL fusion
gene indicate CML.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.3.1.2.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 122 · boc1 PDF page 302

question: Biochemical abnormalities characteristic of polycythemia vera include:
explanation:
Abnormal laboratory findings in polycythemia vera include increased RBC, hemoglobin,
hematocrit, RBC mass and erythropoietin levels.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.2.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 123 · boc1 PDF page 302

question:
A differential cell count of 50-90% myeloblasts in a peripheral blood smear is typical of which
of the following?
explanation:
Laboratory findings indicate >20% myeloblasts, which defines AML.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 124 · boc1 PDF page 303

question: The M:E ratio in acute myelocytic leukemia is usually:
explanation:
A predominance of blasts in AML would increase the M:E ratio.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1] [McKenzie 2020, p587)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 125 · boc1 PDF page 303

question: Which of the following is most closely associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia?
explanation:
DIC is a distinguishing feature of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and often a
presenting condition in patients.
(QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 126 · boc1 PDF page 303

question: Which of the following is most closely associated with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia?
explanation:
Chronic leukemias such as CMML are defined by less than 20% blasts in the peripheral
blood or bone marrow.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.9.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 127 · boc1 PDF page 303

question: Which of the following is most closely associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia?
explanation:
An important feature of CML is the presence of the BCRIABL fusion gene.
(QCMLS 2021 : 14.11]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 128 · boc1 PDF page 303

question: Acute (pure) erythroid leukemia is characterized by the presence of:
options: less than 80% bone marrow erythroid precursors
explanation:
Acute (pure) eythroid leukemia is characterized by >80% immature erythroid precursors
with at least 30% proerythroblasts and myeloblasts.
[QCMLS 2021 : t4.9, 4.9.1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 129 · boc1 PDF page 303

question:
The replacement of normal marrow precursor cells by an accumulation of blasts is a hallmark
of:
explanation:
Acute myelocytic leukemia typically presents with an elevated WBC count because of
numerous circulating blasts. Blasts >20% of all nucleated peripheral blood and bone marrow
cells establishes a diagnosis.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 130 · boc1 PDF page 303

question: All stages of neutrophils are most likely to be seen in the peripheral blood of a patient with:
explanation:
A classic feature of CML is the presence of all stages of granulocyte maturation, as well
as eosinophils and basophils.
[QCMLS 2021 : 14.11]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 131 · boc1 PDF page 303

question: Which of the following conditions is a myeloproliferative neoplasm?
explanation:
Classification of myeloproliferative neoplasms.This category includes CML, CNL, PV,
PMF, ET, chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified, and MPN, unclassifiable.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.3.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 132 · boc1 PDF page 303
