with an increased RBC mass. Peripheral blood findings may include markedly elevated RBC
(and hemoglobin), leukocytosis with granulocytosis and lymphopenia, thrombocytosis, and
elevated uric acid levels. Oxygen saturation is normal.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.3.1.2.2, 14.11) [McKenzie 2020, p537-538]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 133 · boc1 PDF page 304

question: In comparison to malignant lymphocytes, reactive lymphocytes:
options: have more cytoplasm and more mitochondria
are morphologically more variable throughout the smear
explanation:
Reactive lymphocytes are variable in morphology, including variations in size, nuclear
shape and chromatin structure, as well as cytoplasm amount and color.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.3.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 134 · boc1 PDF page 304

question: Which pair of malignancies represent different clinical manifestations of the same disease?
options: chronic lymphocytic leukemia and adult T-cell leukemia
hairy cell leukemia and Hodgkin lymphoma
chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma
explanation:
CLL and SLL represent different clinical presentations of the same disease.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 135 · boc1 PDF page 304

question: Increased levels of TdT activity are indicative of:
explanation:
TdT is a marker for primitive or immature lymphoid cells and is generally negative in acute
myeloid leukemia.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 136 · boc1 PDF page 304

question: Which of the following is true of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)?
options: occurs most commonly in children 1-2 years of age
primitive lymphoid-appearing cells accumulate in bone marrow
children under 1 year of age have a good prognosis
explanation:
Characteristics of ALL include that it is a disease of both young children and adults,
some patients are symptomatic with CNS involvement, the WBC is variable with anemia and
thrombocytopenia typical, the malignant cells are lymphoblasts. Prognosis in children is good,
and fair in adults.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 137 · boc1 PDF page 304

question: The most common form of childhood leukemia is:
explanation:
ALL, notably B cell ALL, is the most common leukemia in children.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.5.1] (McKenzie 2020, p613]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 138 · boc1 PDF page 304

question: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is defined as a(n):
options: accumulation of hairy cells in the spleen
explanation:
CLL is a B cell malignancy of bone marrow and peripheral blood .
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.6.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 139 · boc1 PDF page 304

question: Hairy cell leukemia is a(an):
explanation:
Hairy cell leukemia is a rare condition of lymphocytic origin in which the lymphoid cells
appear to have hair-like projections.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.1.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 140 · boc1 PDF page 305

question: Which of these characteristics is usually associated with hairy cell leukemia?
explanation:
The malignant lymphocytes in hairy cell leukemia characteristically have pale nuclei with
fine chromatin and a pale blue cytoplasm with projections that resemble hairs or may appear
ruffled or frayed.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.6.1.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 141 · boc1 PDF page 305

question: Morphologic variants of plasma cells include:
explanation:
Flame cells are abnormal variants of plasma cells with bright red cytoplasm. They are
associated with plasma cell neoplasms.
[McKenzie 2020, p635]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 142 · boc1 PDF page 305

question: Which of these following bone marrow findings favors the diagnosis of multiple myeloma?
explanation:
Sheets or clusters of plasma cells may be seen in the bone marrow in multiple myeloma.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.2.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 143 · boc1 PDF page 305

question: Which of these clinical conditions has a 8-cell origin?
explanation:
Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a B cell malignancy.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.6.2.5]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 144 · boc1 PDF page 305

question: Which of these cell types is most likely identified in lesions of mycosis fungoides?
explanation:
Mycosis fungoides is related to Sezary syndrome and the neoplastic cells are of T cell
origin.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.2.3)
-------==--------
- - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 145 · boc1 PDF page 305

question: The disease most closely associated with cytoplasmic granule fusion is:
explanation:
Chediak-Higashi syndrome is a disorder of granulocytes that results in the abnormal
fusion of primary and secondary granules.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.8.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 146 · boc1 PDF page 305

question:
Which of these anomalies is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by
irregularly-sized inclusions in polymorphonuclear neutrophils, abnormal giant platelets and
often thrombocytopenia?
explanation:
Peripheral blood findings in May-Hegglin anomaly include irregularly sized inclusions
in (primarily) neutrophils that resemble Dohle bodies, giant or large platelets, and
thrombocytopenia.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.8.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 147 · boc1 PDF page 305

question: The disease most closely associated with granulocyte hyposegmentation is:
explanation:
Pelger-Huet anomaly is a benign disorder in which a morphologic alteration of neutrophils
occurs; the majority of nuclei are bilobed or single and round (nonsegmented or unilobed).
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 148 · boc1 PDF page 305

question: Which of the following is associated with Chediak-Higashi syndrome?
explanation:
Chediak-Higashi syndrome is a disorder of granulocyte membranes that results in the
abnormal fusion of primary (lysosomal) and secondary granules.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.8.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 149 · boc1 PDF page 306

question: Which of the following is associated with Alder-Reilly inclusions?
explanation:
Alder-Reilly anomaly is an inherited condition associated with the
mucopolysaccharidoses and results in abnormal, large azurophilic granules in the cytoplasm
that resemble toxic granulation. These abnormal granules may be seen in all leukocytes but
are most often present in neutrophils.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.8.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 150 · boc1 PDF page 306

question: Which of the following is associated with May-Hegglin anomaly?
explanation:
May-Hegglin anomaly is an inherited disorder in which peripheral blood findings include
irregularly-sized inclusions in (primarily) neutrophils that resemble Dohle bodies, giant or large
platelets, and thrombocytopenia.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 151 · boc1 PDF page 306

question:
A differential is performed on an asymptomatic patient. The differential included
60% neutrophils, 55 of which had 2 lobes and 5 had 3 lobes. There are no other
abnormalities. This is consistent with which of these anomalies?
explanation:
The primary morphologic feature of neutrophils in the Pelger-Huet anomaly is
hyposegmentation, which also may be seen as an acquired condition associated
with MDS/MPN, in COVID-19, and with some drugs.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 152 · boc1 PDF page 306

question:
Patients with chronic granulomatous disease suffer from frequent pyogenic infections due to
the inability of:
options: eosinophils to degranulate in the presence of bacteria
basophils to release histamine in the presence of bacteria
explanation:
CGD is a functional defect of leukocytes in which antimicrobial oxygen metabolites cannot
be produced and intracellular destruction of ingested organisms (phagocytosis) is impaired.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 153 · boc1 PDF page 306

question: Which of the following can cause neutropenia?
explanation:
Causes of leukopenia and neutropenia include several drugs and medications.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.8.1.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 154 · boc1 PDF page 306

question: Which of the following immunohistochemical patterns is most consistent with CLL/SLL?
explanation:
CLL/SLL represent different clinical manifestations of one disease entity. These conditions
are characterized by aberrant expression of the T lymphocyte antigen CD5. Expression of
CD23 is also seen.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.6.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 155 · boc1 PDF page 306

question:
Which of the following morphologic characteristics is consistently associated with hairy cell
leukemia?
explanation:
Hairy cells have characteristicly abundant, pale-staining cytoplasm, cytoplasmic
projections around the circumference of the cell ("hairs"), oval or reniform nuclei, and
relatively fine chromatin.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.1.3)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 156 · boc1 PDF page 306

question:
What is the minimum percentage of prolymphocytes that must be present for a diagnosis of
prolymphocytic leukemia?
explanation:
Prolymphocytes represent >55% of the lymphocytes seen in prolymphocytic leukemia.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.1.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 157 · boc1 PDF page 307

question: Which of the following translocations is most commonly associated with Burkitt lymphoma?
explanation:
Most cases of Burkitt lymphoma are associated with an isolated chromosome
translocation leading to a rearrangement of the MYC and /gH genes, typically t(8;14).
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.7.2, t4.14)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 158 · boc1 PDF page 307

question:
Which of the following genetic alterations is associated with a favorable prognosis in
pre-8-ALL?
MLs
explanation:
The fusion protein produced by the 1(12;21) translocation is associated with a good
prognosis in cases of pre-B cell ALL, with survival rates approaching 90%.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.5.1, 14.13)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 159 · boc1 PDF page 307

question: What is the most common immunoglobulin present in plasma cell myeloma?
explanation:
In plasma cell neoplasms, the monoclonal protein is present in the incidence of lgG,
followed by lgA, lgM, lgD and lgE.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.2.4)
- - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 160 · boc1 PDF page 307

question:
Which of the following is associated with mycosis fungoides?
~lS
explanation:
Sezary cells are malignant T cells in the skin, lymph nodes and peripheral blood. These
cells may also be seen in a primary cutaneous T cell lymphoma called mycosis fungoides.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.6.2.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 161 · boc1 PDF page 307

question: Which of the following is a characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: high incidence of peripheral blood infiltration
explanation:
A bimodal age distribution is seen in Hodgkin lymphoma, with a peak incidence in 15-35
year olds and again in patients over 50.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.7.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 162 · boc1 PDF page 307

question: Which of the following is suggestive of a myeloproliferative disorder?
explanation:
In the WHO classification system, myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are characterized
by panmyelosis of the bone marrow and peripheral blood erythrocytosis, granulocytosis and/or
thrombocytosis.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 163 · boc1 PDF page 307

question: Which of the following is characteristic of the myelodysplastic syndromes?
explanation:
Dysplastic features in one or more cell lines are typical in the myelodysplastic syndromes
(MOS).
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 164 · boc1 PDF page 307

question: Which of the following is a WHO classification of myelodysplastic syndrome?
explanation:
The subgroups of MOS include MOS with single lineage dysplasia, MOS with single
lineage dysplasia and ringeds sideroblasts, MOS with multilineage dysplasia, MOS
with multilineage dysplasis and ringed sideroblasts, MOS with excess blasts, MOS with
isolated del (Sq), MOS, unclassifiable, and refractory cytopenia of childhood. Refractory
thrombocytopenia is included in the category of refractory cytopenia with single lineage
dysplasia.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.2, t4.1 OJ
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 165 · boc1 PDF page 307

question:
Which of the following cytogenetic abnormalities is associated with a more stable clinical
course in myelodysplastic syndromes (MDSs)?
explanation:
Patients who have MOS with isolated deletion of chromosome Sq have long-term stable
disease.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 166 · boc1 PDF page 308

question:
Which of the following disorders is a category in the WHO classification of myelodysplastic
syndromes/myeloproliferative neoplasms?
explanation:
The classification of myelodysplastic syndromes/myeloproliferative neoplasms
comprises chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, atypical chronic myeloid leukemia, juvenile
myelomonocytic leukemia and myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm, unclassifiable.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 167 · boc1 PDF page 308

question: Which of the following features define chronic myelogenous leukemia?
explanation:
The Philadelphia chromosome is an acquired translocation between the long arms of
chromosomes 9 and 22 and is associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.8.1.2, 14.11]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 168 · boc1 PDF page 308

question:
Which of the following are main groups of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in the WHO
classification system?
explanation:
The 2008 WHO classification of AML. AML, NOS (not otherwise specified) is a category of
AML as defined by the WHO.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 169 · boc1 PDF page 308

question:
What type of morphologically abnormal cells proliferate in acute myelogenous leukemia with
inv(16)?
explanation:
AML with inv(16)(p13;q22) generally presents with monocytic and granulocytic maturation
along with abnormal eosinophils in the bone marrow.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1 .2, t4.9]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 170 · boc1 PDF page 308

question: What defines acute myelogenous leukemia with minimal differentiation?
options: >20% blasts positive for Sudan black B
positivity for myeloperoxidase or nonspecific esterase in at least 50% of blasts
positivity for myeloperoxidase or nonspecific esterase in at least 100% of blasts
>20% blasts lacking cytochemical evidence of myeloid differentiation
explanation:
WHO criteria for AML indicate that blasts must comprise ~20% of nonerythroid
nucleated cells in acute leukemia. AML with minimal differentiation is characterized by no
evidence of morphologic myeloid maturation (no granules) and <3% of blasts positive for
myeloperoxidase.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1.2)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 171 · boc1 PDF page 308

question: What is the most common presentation of acute erythroid leukemia?
options: >80% of nucleated marrow cells are erythroid precursors

>50% of nucleated marrow cells are erythroid precursors and >20% of nonerythroid cells
are myeloblasts

>50% of nucleated marrow cells are erythroid precursors and <20% of nonerythroid cells
are myeloblasts
explanation:
There are 2 variants of acute erythroid leukemia distinguished by the presence or
absence of myeloblasts. The erythroid/myeloid variant is seen when ~50% of nucleated
cells in the bone marrow are erythroid precursors and ~20% of the nonerythroid cells are
myeloblasts. Pure erythroid leukemia is confirmed when >80% on nucleated cells in the bone
marrow are erythroid precursors. Pure erythroid leukemia is rare.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 172 · boc1 PDF page 308

question: Which of the following is associated with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia?
explanation:
Children with Down syndrome have a 50x greater risk of developing acute myeloid
leukemia (AML). The abnormal cells are megakaryoblasts. This condition is a category in the
WHO classification of AML designated as Myeloid Proliferations Related to Down Syndrome.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.12]
-
~ - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 173 · boc1 PDF page 308

question:
Which of the following cell surface markers is associated with a more aggressive subtype of
CLUSLL?
explanation:
More aggressive cases of CLL are associated with higher levels of CD38.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.1.1)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 174 · boc1 PDF page 309

question: The leukemic phase of T cell lymphoma is marked by the following cellular abnormality:
explanation:
Sezary cells are neoplastic T lymphocytes associated with Sezary syndrome and primary
cutaneous T cell lymphoma.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.6.2.3)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 175 · boc1 PDF page 309

question:
A bone marrow shows foam cells ranging from 20-100 µm, vacuolated cytoplasm containing
~fy sphingomyelin and faint PAS positivity. This cell type is most characteristic of:
explanation:
Foam cells with sphingomyelin and PAS positivity mark the classic morphology of
Niemann-Pick cells.
[McKenzie 2015, p403]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 176 · boc1 PDF page 309

question: A useful chemical test for the diagnosis of hairy cell leukemia is the:
explanation:
TRAP stain positivity is characteristic of hairy cell leukemia.
[QCMLS 2011: 4.9.6.1.3) [Glassy 2018, p300]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 177 · boc1 PDF page 309

question: Aspirin affects platelet function by interfering with platelets' metabolism of:
explanation:
Aspirin interferes with prostaglandin metabolism in the platelet by inhibiting
cyclooxygenase, which participates in the conversion of arachidonic acid to protein G2;
protein G2 is necessary to produce thromboxane, which stimulates secretion from the platelet
granules.

question:
In patients who present with bleeding disorders caused by platelets, the most common type of
bleeding is:
explanation:
Certain characteristics of platelet-type bleeding disorders include mucosa! bleeding,
petechiae, and a female predominance. Other types of bleeding are due to defects in
coagulation factors. Hemarthrosis and deep hematomas occur in Factor VIII deficiency
(hemophilia), delayed bleeding occurs in Factor XIII deficiency, and deep hematomas present
with the other choices in the question.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.5)

question:
The anticoagulant that is best directed against platelets is:
I.ILS
explanation:
Hirudin, argatroban and dabigatran are direct thrombin inhibitors. They are either isolated
from the leech, Hirudo medicinalis (hirudin), or are recombinant forms of the same protein
(lepirudin, argatroban, dabigatran). Tirofiban is not related and is a platelet GPllb/llla inhibitor
and is an anti-platelet drug.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.5.2.4)

explanation:

blunted ADP response with aggregometry studies, but normal results with other agonists.

[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.5.2.4)

explanation:
vWF binds platelets through their GP lb/lXN membrane receptor. The importance of
platelet adhesion is demonstrated by bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease,
in which vWF is missing or defective, and Bernard Soulier disease, in which the GP lb/lXN
receptor is absent.

explanation:

~fv with heparin therapy. Antibodies are produced against:
explanation:

question: Large blue inclusions bodies in WBC are found in patients with:
explanation:
May-Hegglin anomaly is a rare, autosomal dominant platelet disorder. Patients present
with variable thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and large Dohle body-like inclusions
in the neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and monocytes. The majority of patients are
asymptomatic, but a few have shown mild bleeding tendencies related to the degree of
thrombocytopenia. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome are both
disorders of platelet secretion, specifically storage pool disorders. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
is a vascular disorder in which a bleeding tendency is manifested primarily in subcutaneous
hematoma formation.

What is the best course of action?
options: determine how the samples were collected
determine if the samples are from the same patient
consider a redraw of the specimen

reference methods is the method of choice for validation.
[Rodak 2016, p224]

question:
Blood is diluted 1 :200, and a platelet count is performed. 180 platelets are counted in the
center square millimeter on one side of the hemacytometer and 186 on the other side.
The total platelet count is:
explanation:
Average the number of cells counted on both sides of the chamber, then use the formula:
total count = number of cells counted (average of both sides) x dilution factor divided by the
area counted (mm2) x depth.
[QCMLS 2021 4.10.1) [Rodak 2020, p158]

A phase-platelet count is performed and the total platelet count is 356,000/µL (3.56 x 1012/L).
Ten high power (1 00x) fields on the stained blood smear are examined for platelets and the
results per field were:
1~ 18, 15,2~ 19, 1i 19, 18, 20, 16
The next step would be to:
options: report the phase-platelet count since it correlated well with the slide
repeat the phase-platelet count on a recollected specimen and check for clumping
check 10 additional fields on the blood smear
repeat the platelet count using a different method
explanation:
The platelet count matches the estimate well. The average number of platelets per 1 00x
oil immersion field (17.8 in this case) x 20,000 approximates the platelet count.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.4.3] [Rodak 2020, p207]

Which hematology manufacturer uses multi-angle polarized scatter separation (MAPSS) and
fluorescence to perform a WBC differential?

Abbott instruments combine several technologies to count and identify blood cells.
MAPPS is the primary, patented method that generates data used to classify leukocyte
subpopulations.
[Rodak 2020, p178; McKenzie 2020, p980-981]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 237 · boc1 PDF page 322

explanation:
This scatter plot represents a normal display of cell populations as generated by a
Siemens Advia instrument. The channel shown identifies white blood cell populations based
on light scatter and peroxidase staining. The position of the numeral 6 indicates the location
of monocytes.
[McKenzie 2020, p986]
B. Differentials and Morphology Evaluation

question:
In which of the following disease states are teardrop cells and abnormal platelets most
characteristically seen?
explanation:
Primary myelofibrosis presents with dacryocytes (teardrop cells) nucleated RBCs and
megakaryocytic fragments. A clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by ineffective
hematopoiesis associated with bone marrow hypercellularity, extra-medullary hematopoiesis,
fibrosis and increased megakaryocytes.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.3.1.3, i4.37] [Rodak 2020, p574-576]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 239 · boc1 PDF page 323

question: Which of the following represent residual nuclear fragments?
explanation:
· Cabot rings are believed to be remnants of spindle fibers formed during mitosis. They
can be in ring or figure-eight forms. They are associated with megaloblastic anemia and
myelodysplasic syndromes.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.4.2, t4.18] [Rodak 2020 p256]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 240 · boc1 PDF page 323

question:
Which of the following RBC inclusions are seen in sideroblastic anemia and contain high
amounts of iron?
explanation:
RBCs in sideroblastic anemia can contain iron deposits known as Pappenheimer bodies.
Pappenheimer bodies are irregular clusters of small light to dark granules found near the
periphery of the red blood cell (with Wright stain). They can also be stained with Prussian
blue for iron. They can be seen in hemoglobinopathies, thalassemias, megaloblastic anemia,
myelodysplasia, hyposplenism, and postsplenectomy.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.4.2, 14.18] [Rodak 2020, p256]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 241 · boc1 PDF page 323

question:
The nucleated cell in the photomicrograph may be seen in the peripheral blood of a normal
newborn and is classified as a(an):
explanation:
The round nucleus, pyknotic or condensed chromatin and abundant gray-pink cytoplasm
with nearly complete hemoglobin production are characteristic of the orthochromatic
normoblast (metarubricyte ).
[Gulati 2021, p23; Rodak 2020, p68-69]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 242 · boc1 PDF page 324

question:
A Wright-stained peripheral blood smear reveals blue, ring-shaped inclusions with red
chromatin dots in several of the red blood cells. These inclusions are consistent with:
explanation:
Malarial parasites, especially Falciparum species, commonly appear on a Wright-stained
peripheral blood slide as small blue rings with a red nucleus or chromatin dot.
(QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.4.2, 14.18]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 243 · boc1 PDF page 324

question: A red blood cell about 5 µm in diameter that stains bright red and shows no central pallor is a:
explanation:
Spherocytes are small, round, dense RBCs with no central pallor. Sometimes they occur
with a high MCHC. They are associated with hereditary spherocytosis, immune hemolytic
anemia, and extensive burns.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.4.2, 14.18] [Rodak 2020, p255]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 244 · boc1 PDF page 324

Examination of a Wright-stained smear of the same sample would most likely show:
explanation:
A calculation of the RBC indices can be used to classify anemia. The MCV determines
the volume or size of the cell. If the MCV is <80 fl the RBCs are referred to as microcytic; if
> 100 fl, macrocytic; and if 80-100 fl, normocytic. The MCHC refers to the concentration of
hemoglobin in the RSC. If the MCHC is <32 g/dl the RBCs are referred to as hypochromic;
if 32-36 g/dl, normochromic
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.8) [Rodak 2020, p163-164]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 245 · boc1 PDF page 324

question: Evidence of active red cell regeneration may be indicated on a blood smear by:
options: nucleated red blood cells and polychromasia
basophilic stippling and nucleated red blood cells
explanation:
Nucleated RBCs and polychromasia can be associated with accelerated RBC production.
The polychromatic RBC has no nucleus and is the last stage before becoming a mature
erythrocyte. Other immature (nucleated) RBCs may be seen in the peripheral blood as
an indicator that the bone marrow is producing and releasing erythrocytes in an effort to
regenerate cells that are being lost as a result of many possible mechanisms.
[McKenzie 2020, p210]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 246 · boc1 PDF page 324

question: The smear represented in the photomicrograph displays:
explanation:
HbC crystals can be seen in patients with HbC disease. Hemoglobin C crystals are
rigid and hexagonal in shape. They can be seen as intracellular inclusions when RBCs are
dehydrated. Crystals are densely stained and vary in size. Hemoglobin C disease presents
with a mild to moderate normochromic, normocytic anemia.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.7.3) [Rodak 2020, p411-412]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 247 · boc1 PDF page 325

question:
The presence of excessive rouleaux formation on a blood smear is often accompanied by an
increased:
explanation:
Rouleaux formation occurs when plasma proteins are increased and results in an
elevated ESR. Rouleaux represents aggregation of stacked RBCs caused by elevated plasma
proteins and abnormal monoclonal proteins as seen in multiple myeloma.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.11.1, 4.9.6.2.4) [Rodak 2020, p169, 619]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 248 · boc1 PDF page 325

question: The characteristic peripheral blood morphologic feature in multiple myeloma is:
explanation:
The peripheral smear allows microscopic examination of the blood cells. The most
characteristic finding in multiple myeloma is rouleaux formation of the red cells. An abnormal
and excess number of plasma cells secrete monoclonial immunoglobins that allow red blood
cells to form rouleaux.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.2.4) [Rodak 2020, p619]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 249 · boc1 PDF page 325

question:
Many microspherocytes, schistocytes and spherocytes with budding cytoplasm can be seen
on peripheral blood smears of patients with:
explanation:
Patients who have suffered severe burns to >15% of their body generally show evidence
of intravascular hemolysis. RBCs show changes including fragmentation, budding and
microspherocyte formation.
[McKenzie 2020, p188; Rodak 2020, p373]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 250 · boc1 PDF page 325

question: The light-colored zone adjacent to the nucleus in a plasma cell is the:
explanation:
Plasma cells are cells with eccentric dark nuclei, blue cytoplasm, and a prominent, pale,
central Golgi apparatus. The chromatin in the nucleus may have a clock face appearance.
[QCMLS 2021 4.9.6.2.4, i4.47) [Rodak 2020, p232]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 251 · boc1 PDF page 325

question: Inclusions in the cytoplasm of neutrophils as shown in the photomicrograph are known as:
explanation:
Dahle bodies are light blue, usually single inclusions of varying sizes. They are seen in
the cytoplasm of neutrophils and bands and are remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Dahle bodies are often associated with toxic granulation and toxic vacuoles.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.4.1) [Rodak 2020, p457-458]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 252 · boc1 PDF page 326

question: The term "shift to the left" refers to:
options: immature cell forms in the peripheral blood
a trend on a Levy-Jennings chart
a calibration adjustment on an instrument
explanation:
The term "left shift" is based on the use of old-style cell counters, which had keys for
immature neutrophils to the left of those for mature neutrophils. A left shift is defined as an
increase in the production of neutrophils in the bone marrow or as a transfer of neutrophils
from the bone marrow storage pool to the circulation pool. Immature cells will increase, and
will include bands, metamyelocytes, and myelocytes.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.1.1) [Rodak 2020, p454-455]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 253 · boc1 PDF page 326

question:
A term that means varying degrees of leukocytosis with a shift to the left and occasional
nucleated red cells in the peripheral blood is:
explanation:
Leukoerythroblastosis is characterized by an increase in the WBC count and the
presence of immature red blood cells and granulocytes in the peripheral blood and bone
marrow. Leukoerythroblastosis is seen in primary myelofibrosis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.3.1.J] [Rodak 2020, p454, 576, 858)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 254 · boc1 PDF page 326

question: In the photomicrograph the small nucleated cell seen in the lower left corner is a:
explanation:
Mature (resting) lymphocytes are small with a round nucleus and scant blue cytoplasm.
The chromatin pattern is arranged in blocks, and the nucleolus is rarely seen.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.4.1, t4.17) [Rodak 2020, p130-131]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 255 · boc1 PDF page 326

question: The large cells seen in the photomicrograph are most consistent with:
explanation:
Reactive changes in lymphocyte morphology occur when lymphocytes are stimulated,
often in response to viral infection, as in infectious mononucleosis. Reative lymphocytes vary
in size and shape. The nucleus is irregular with less condensed chromatin. Nucleoli may be
seen. The cytoplasm is abundant and basophilic with darker edges, and they may be indented
by surrounding RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021 4.8.3.1, 14.17, 14.8] [Rodak 2020, p460-461]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 256 · boc1 PDF page 327

question: The cell in the center of the photomicrograph is a:
explanation:
Monocytes appear larger than neutrophils (15-20 µm). The nucleus may be round, oval,
or kidney or horseshoe shapes. The nucleus tends to be folded on itself with a chromatin
pattern that is loose, often described as lacy. Nucleoli are usually not seen. The cytoplasm
is blue-gray and may appear like ground glass. Sometimes fine azure granules and vacuoles
may be seen. Small cytoplastic pseudopods or blebs may also be seen.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.4.1, 14.17] [Rodak 2020, p128]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 257 · boc1 PDF page 327

question: The large cell in the center of the photomicrograph would be best described as a(n):
explanation:
Mature basophils contain a lobulated (typically 2 lobes) nucleus. The chromatin pattern
if visible is usually clumped. The cytoplasm is colorless to pinkish and contains numerous,
large, blue-black granules which often obscure the nucleus.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.4.1, 14.16] [Rodak 2020, p126]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 258 · boc1 PDF page 328

question: The large cell indicated by the arrow in the photomicrograph is a:
explanation:
Promyelocytes are large cells with a high N:C ratio. The nucleus is round or oval and 2
or more nucleoli may be visible. The cytoplasm is basophilic and characteristically has few
to numerous prominent, dark red or purple primary granules.
(QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.4.1, t4.16)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 259 · boc1 PDF page 328

question:
A patient is diagnosed as having bacterial septicemia. Which of the following would best
describe the expected change in his peripheral blood?
explanation:
A granulocytic leukemoid reaction is also known as a reactive neutrophilia in which
the WBC count is very elevated with a shift to the left. The condition occurs in response
to a nonmalignant condition such as a bacterial infection or inflammation. Neutrophils and
immature neutrophil forms may be seen.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.8.11] [Rodak 2020, p454, 863]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 260 · boc1 PDF page 328

question: Characteristic morphologic features of reactive lymphocytes include:
options: small size, clumped nuclear chromatin, scanty basophilic cytoplasm
large cell, oval nucleus, scanty blue-gray cytoplasm
large size, irregularly shaped nucleus, abundant blue cytoplasm
explanation:
Reactive changes in lymphocyte morphology occur when lymphocytes are stimulated.
Reactive lymphocytes vary in size and shape. The nucleus is irregular with less condensed
chromatin. Nucleoli may be seen. The cytoplasm is abundant and basophilic with darker
edges that may be indented by surrounding RBCs.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.8.3.1, i4.25, t4.8] [Rodak 2020 p460-461]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 261 · boc1 PDF page 328

question: If a blood smear is dried too slowly, the red blood cells are often:
explanation:
Blood smears should be dried quickly to avoid drying artifacts.
[Rodak 2020, p204]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 262 · boc1 PDF page 328

question:
The specimen of choice for preparation of blood films for manual differential leukocyte counts
is whole blood collected in:
explanation:
High-quality blood smears can be made from an EDTA tube within 4 hours of drawing
the specimen. After 5 hours cell artifacts develop. EDTA generally prevents platelets from
clumping on glass slides.
[Rodak 2020, p202]

question:
On a smear made directly from a finger stick, no platelets are found in the counting area.
The first thing to do is:
explanation:
Platelet clumping is expected if smears are made directly from the finger stick draw.
Smears must be made promptly before any clotting begins and should be prepared at the
patient's bedside. It is important to examine the edges of the slide for platelet clumping.
[Rodak 2020, p202-203]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 264 · boc1 PDF page 329

question:
Evidence of a hemolytic event is present in the peripheral blood smear when which of the
following is seen?
explanation:
In a hemolytic event, the blood smear may reveal polychromasia as evidence of bone
marrow compensation for anemia.
[Gulati 2021, p24)
C. Hemoglobin
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 265 · boc1 PDF page 329

question: A common source of interference in measuring hemoglobin concentration is:
explanation:
A very high WBC count (>20,000) or a high platelet count (>700,000) in
cyanmethemoglobin reagent-treated specimens causes turbidity, which will result in
falsely-elevated hemoglobin values.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.1.2) [Rodak 2020, p161)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 266 · boc1 PDF page 329

question: A patient with beta-thalassemia characteristically has a(n):
explanation:
In beta-thalassemia minor the HbA2 level is 3-7% and HbF is <5%. In beta-thalassemia
major HbA is absent or decreased, HbA2 is variable but HbF is at 70%. Thalassemia presents
with microcytic RBCs and usually a normal iron.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.1.2) [Rodak 2020, p431-432)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 267 · boc1 PDF page 329

question: An additional test indicated by the photomicrograph is:
explanation:
HbC crystals are hexagonal in shape, stain densely, and vary in size and shape.
They appear oblong and have rounded ends. Definitive diagnosis is via electrophoresis.
HbC crystals can be seen in patients with HbC disease, but the condition must be confirmed
with hemoglobin electrophoresis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.7.3) [Rodak 2020, p412)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 268 · boc1 PDF page 329

question: The most appropriate screening test for hemoglobin S is:
explanation:
The most common screening test for HbS is called the hemoglobin solubility test, which
capitalizes on the decreased solubility of deoxygenated hemoglobin when in solution,
producing a turbidity. The confirmation test is hemoglobin electrophoresis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.6.1) [Rodak 2020, p406]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 269 · boc1 PDF page 330

question: Which of the following is characteristic of hemoglobin H?
options: it is a tetramer of gamma chains
it has a lower oxygen affinity than hemoglobin A
explanation:
Deletion of 3 alpha globins results in HbH. It is characterized by the accumulation of
excess beta chains.HbH is a fast-migrating hemoglobin.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.6.2) [Rodak 2020, p435-436)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 270 · boc1 PDF page 330

question: In most cases of hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH):
options: hemoglobin F is unevenly distributed throughout the erythrocytes
the black heterozygote has 75% hemoglobin F
beta- and gamma-chain synthesis is decreased
explanation:
HPFH results when there is either a deletion or inactivation of the beta and gamma gene
complex. There is a delayed switch from gamma to beta or delta production with no HbA or
HbA2 produced. HbF persists into adulthood. Both gamma and alpha chains are produced in
approximately equal amounts.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.7.9] [McKenzie 2020, p309-310)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 271 · boc1 PDF page 330

question:
When using the turbidity (solubility) method for detecting the presence of hemoglobin S,
~tY an incorrect interpretation may be made when there is a(n):
explanation:
Anemia, as indicated by a decreased hematocrit, may result in a falsely negative result
because the amount of HbS is too low to be accurately detected.
[McKenzie 2020, p277]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 272 · boc1 PDF page 330

question:
A native of Thailand has a normal hemoglobin level. Hemoglobin electrophoresis on cellulose
acetate shows 70% HbA and approximately 30% of a hemoglobin with the mobility of HbA2.
This is most consistent with hemoglobin:
explanation:
HbE has a high incidence in Southeast Asia and migrates with HbA2, HbC and HbOArab
on cellulose acetate electrophoresis.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.6.2] [Rodak 2020 412-413]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 275 · boc1 PDF page 331

question: Automated methods of measuring hemoglobin cannot detect this form:
explanation:
In the cyanmethhemoglobin method, hemoglobin is oxidized to methemoglobin (Fe3+)
by potassium ferricyanide, and is then converted to cyanmethoglobin by potassium cyanide.
The cyanmethemoglobin concentration is directly proportional to hemoglobin concentration.
Sulfhemoglobin is not converted to cyanmethemoglobin and cannot be measured by this
method.
[Rodak 2020, p160]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 276 · boc1 PDF page 331

question:
In the hemoglobin solubility (dithionate) test, which type of hemoglobin causes turbidity
(positive reaction)?
explanation:
The solubility test is a common procedure used to screen for the presence of HbS.
The principle of the procedure involves the insolubility of HbS when RBCs are added to
a solution of sodium hydrosulfite (sodium dithionite). The reagent lyses RBCs to release
hemoglobin and then reduces the hemoglobin, which then forms tactoids when HbS is
present. The solution becomes cloudy (turbid), indicating a positive reaction.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.6.2] [Rodak 2020, p406]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 277 · boc1 PDF page 331

question: The presence of HbH may be demonstrated by:
explanation:
HbH inclusions are seen after incubation of blood with brilliant cresyl blue. The inclusions
give the RBC the appearance of a golf ball.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.1.2] [Rodak 2020, p438]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 278 · boc1 PDF page 331

question:
The hemoglobin variant that is seen frequently in the South East Asian population,
demonstrates a microcytic blood smear, and migrates with HbC at pH 8.6 is:
explanation:
On alkaline electrophoresis, HbE migrates with HbA2, HbC and HbOArab· HbE is seen
commonly in Southeast Asia and presents with a microcytic,hypochromic anemia.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.7.5] [Rodak 2020, p412-413]
D. Hematocrit
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 279 · boc1 PDF page 331

question:
Automated hematology analyzers calculate the hematocrit using which of the following
parameters?
explanation:
Most automated instruments determine the hematocrit using the directly measured
MCV and RBC count with the formula: MCV (fl) x RBC (x1012/L)/1000. Sysmex uses the
cumulative detection of RBC pulse heights.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.7.2] [Rodak 2020, p178]
--"----=-----=-=---
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 280 · boc1 PDF page 332

question: A false elevation in a manual hematocrit (microhematocrit) determination may result from:
options: incomplete sealing of the hematocrit tube
explanation:
The trapping of plasma causes the microhematocrit to be 1-3% higher than the value
obtained using automation. Sickle cell anemia, macrocytic anemias, hypochromic anemias,
spherocytes and thalassemia may cause plasma to be trapped in the RBC layer. Other errors
may result through improper sample collection and handling or when the procedure is not
followed correctly.
(QCMLS 4.10.7.1) [Rodak 2020, p162]
E. Indices
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 281 · boc1 PDF page 332

question: What cell shape is most commonly associated with an increased MCHC?
explanation:
Spherocytes are RBCs without central pallor (due to decreased RBC membrane) and
often have a high MCHC. Spherocytes may be referred to as hyperchromic because of
increased MCHC.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.4.2, 14.18) [Rodak 2020, p255]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 282 · boc1 PDF page 332

question:
Which of the RBC indices is a measure of the amount of hemoglobin in individual red blood
cells?
explanation:
The MCH is the average weight of hemoglobin in a RBC, expressed in picograms (pg).
The formula to calculate the MCH is: hemoglobin x 10 divided by the RBC count.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.8.1) [Rodak 2020, p164)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 283 · boc1 PDF page 332

question:
The ROW-CV and ROW-SD performed by automated hematology analyzers are calculations
that provide:
options: an index of the distribution of RBC volumes
a calculated mean RBC hemoglobin concentration
explanation:
The ROW is the coefficient of variation of RBC volume expressed as a percent.
It indicates the variation in the RBC volume (size) and correlates with anisocytosis.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.8.1) (Rodak 2020, p254]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 284 · boc1 PDF page 332

A stained blood film of this patient would most likely reveal a red cell picture that is:
explanation:
In determining the appearance of RBCs for classification of anemia, the MCV and the
MCHC are usually used. When the MCV <80 fl the cell is microcytic; when >100 fl the
cell is macrocytic. When the MCHC <32 g/dl the cell is hypochromic. The MCH may also
sometimes be used to classify anemia. When the MCH is <28 pg, the cell is hypochromic.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.8.2) [Rodak 2020, p163]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 285 · boc1 PDF page 332

The MCV is calculated using the formula: hematocrit x 10 divided by the RBC count. It is
commonly expressed in femtoliters (fl).
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.8.1) [Rodak 2020, p164)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 286 · boc1 PDF page 333

question: Which of these formulas is used for calculating the mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH)?
explanation:
The MCH is calculated using the formula: hemoglobin x 10 divided by the RBC count and
is measured in picograms (pg).
(QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.8.1) (Rodak 2020, p163]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 287 · boc1 PDF page 333

question:
What is the MCH if the HCT is 20%, the RBC is 2.4 x 106/µl (2.4 x 1012/l) and
the HGB is 5 g/dl (50 g/l)?
explanation:
The MCH is calculated using the formula: hemoglobin x 10 divided by the RBC count and
is measured in picograms (pg).
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.8.1) [Rodak 2020, p163)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 288 · boc1 PDF page 333

question: Which of these formulas is used for calculating the MCHC?
explanation:
The MCHC is calculated using the formula HBG x 100 / HCT. It is expressed in grams per
deciliter (g/dl).
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.8.1) [Rodak 2020, p163]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 289 · boc1 PDF page 333

question:
What is the MCHC if the HCT is 20%, the RBC is 2.4 x 106/µl (2.4 x 1012/l ) and
the HGB is 5 g/dl (50 g/l)?
explanation:
The MCHC is calculated using the formula HBG x 100 / HCT. It is expressed in grams per
deciliter (g/dl).
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.8.1) (Rodak 2020, p163]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 290 · boc1 PDF page 333

question: Which of these formulas is used for calculating the mean corpuscular volume (MCV)?
explanation:
The MCV is calculated using the formula HCT x 10 / RBC count. It is expressed in
femtoliters (fl).
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.8.1) [Rodak 2020, p163)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 291 · boc1 PDF page 333

question:
The calculated erythrocyte indices on an adult man are MCV = 89 fl, MCH = 29 pg and
~tv MCHC = 38%. The calculations have been rechecked; erythrocytes on the peripheral blood
smear appear normocytic and normochromic with no abnormal forms. The next step is to:
options: repeat the erythrocyte count and hematocrit
explanation:
An MCHC >38 g/dl should be investigated for an error in determining the hemoglobin
value. False increases in MCHC can occur when hemoglobin and hematocrit values are
spuriously affected as these parameters are used to calculate the MCHC.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.8.1) [Rodak 2020, p163]
F Hemolytic Indicators
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 292 · boc1 PDF page 333

question: Which of these laboratory findings is associated with extravascular hemolysis?
explanation:
Bilirubin results from increased heme catabolism and will be increased in extravascular
hemolysis. Microcytes are associated with anemias related to defects in hemoglobin
synthesis, and hemoglobinuria is associated with intravascular hemolysis. RBC membrane
structural defects result in rigid cells, like spherocytes, which are less able to negotiate the
small passages of the spleen and result in extravascular hemolysis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.6.3, 4.7.1.3.1.1, t4.18) [Rodak 2020, p329]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 293 · boc2 PDF page 1

question: One of the major differences between extravascular and intravascular hemolysis is:
explanation:
Extravascular hemolysis accounts for 90% of RBC destruction, occurs primarily in the
spleen, and involves the key breakdown products of heme, iron, and globin. lntravascular
hemolysis is responsible for 10% of RBC destruction; however, the lysis is visible in the
peripheral blood (circulation) as free hemoglobin.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.6.3)

source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 294 · boc2 PDF page 1

Examination of the bone marrow reveals the absence of iron stores. This data is most

explanation:
Laboratory findings in iron deficiency anemia include decreased serum iron, serum

[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.1.1) [Rodak 2020, p268-269]

Examination of the bone marrow reveals erythroid hyperplasia with a shift to the left of
erythroid precursors. Prussian blue staining reveals markedly elevated iron stores noted
with occasional sideroblasts seen. This data is most consistent with which of the following
conditions?
explanation:
Hemochromatosis is iron overload. It can be primary, as in hereditary hemochromatosis,
or secondary, due to chronic anemia or treatments such as multiple transfusions. Secondary
hemochromatosis is associated with anemia and abnormally high serum iron studies.
Prussian blue is the stain for iron.
[QCMLS 2021: 2.10.2.1.3) [Rodak 2020, p274-275]

question: A screening procedure for detecting hemoglobin F is the:
explanation:
The Kleihauer-Betke procedure is commonly used as a screening test to determine the
amount of fetal blood that has mixed with maternal blood. Blood smears are immersed in
an acid buffer, which causes HgA to be eluted form the RBCs. The smear is stained and the
RBCs that contain fetal hemoglobin take up the stain. This stain can be used in assessing
hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH), fetal maternal hemorrhage, and beta
thalassemia.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.3) [Rodak 2020, p858]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 297 · boc2 PDF page 2

question: The Prussian blue staining of peripheral blood identifies:
explanation:
Siderocytes (and sideroblasts) may be identified with the Prussian blue iron stain, which
stains iron deposits. Siderocytes are RBCs that have no nuclei but contain iron. When the iron
surrounds the nucleus of immature RBCs, the cells are called ringed sideroblasts.
[Rodak 2020, p273]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 298 · boc2 PDF page 2

question: Which of the following stains is used to demonstrate iron, ferritin and hemosiderin?
explanation:
The Prussian blue stain is used for assessing iron stores in bone marrow.Prussian blue is
considered the gold standard for the assessment of iron stores.
[QCMLS 2021 4.10.5.2) [Rodak 2020, p111]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 299 · boc2 PDF page 2

question:
Which of the following stains can be used to differentiate siderotic granules
(Pappenheimer bodies) from basophilic stippling?
explanation:
The Prussian blue stain is used to differentiate siderotic (iron) granules (Pappenheimer
bodies) from basophilic stippling. The term "Pappenheimer" describes these granules when
viewed in RBCs with a Wright stain. The term "siderocyte" describes the granules in RBCs
when Prussian blue is used. Pappenheimer bodies are composed of iron; basophilic stipping
is composed of precipitated RNA.
(QCMLS 2021: 14.18] [Rodak 2020, p256 116.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 300 · boc2 PDF page 2

question: Which cell type shows the most intense staining with myeloperoxidase?
explanation:
Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is an enzyme found in the primary granules of granulocytic cells.
Lymphocytes do not exhibit MPO. The stain is used to differentiate AML from ALL.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.1) [Rodak 2020, p549]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 301 · boc2 PDF page 3

question: Which substrate is used for the detection of specific esterase?
explanation:
Esterases are used to differentiate myeloblasts from cells of monocytic origin.
Alpha-naphthyl acetate and alpha-naphthyl butyrate are nonspecific esterases. Naphthol
AS-D chloroacetate is a specific esterase, which means that only granulocytic cells show
staining. The nonspecific esterase stains monocytic cells, while granulocytes are negative.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.1] [Rodak 2020, p550]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 302 · boc2 PDF page 3

question:
A myeloperoxidase stain and immunophenotyping are performed on bone marrow smears
from a patient diagnosed with an acute leukemia. The myeloperoxidase is positive and
immunophenotyping shows positivity for CD4, CD13, CD11b, CD13, CD33 and CD64.
What type of leukemia is indicated?
explanation:
Myeloperoxidase is positive, along with chloroacetate, both of which are granulocytic
markers. Alpha-naphthyl acetate is also positive and indicates cells of monocytic origin are
present. Blasts that are positive for all the stains suggest the presence of both myeloblasts
and monoblasts, or the diagnosis of a myelomonocytic leukemia.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.1) [Rodak 2020, p549-551)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 303 · boc2 PDF page 3

question:
Which of the following stains is closely associated with the lysosomal enzyme in primary
(azurophilic) granules?
explanation:
Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is an enzyme found in the primary granules of granulocytic cells.
Lymphocytes do not exhibit MPO. The stain is used to differentiate AML from ALL.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.1) (Rodak 2020, p549)

question: Heinz bodies are:
explanation:
The composition of Heinz bodies is denatured hemoglobin; these inclusions and are not
seen with Wright stain. They are associated with a G6PD deficiency.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.10.4) [Rodak 2020, p256)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 305 · boc2 PDF page 3

question:
Which of the following technical factors will cause a normal (low) erythrocyte sedimentation
rate?
options: small fibrin clots in the sample
explanation:
Specimen handling and technical factors can affect the ESR. A clotted specimen and
delay in testing will decrease the ESR.
[Rodak 2020, p168-169]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 306 · boc2 PDF page 3

question: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) can be falsely elevated by:
explanation:
A falsely-elevated ESR can be caused by high room temperature, tilting of the tube,
and vibration.
[Rodak 2020, p168-169)

source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 307 · boc2 PDF page 3

question: A confirmatory test for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is:
explanation:
PNH is an acquired clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder; it results in a rare, chronic,
intravascular hemolytic anemia. Blood cell membranes are missing GPl-anchored proteins
designated CD55 and CD59. Absence of these proteins causes the RBCs to be lysed by
complement. lnmmunophenotyping is the confirmatory testing method and typically uses
fluorescent monoclonal antibodies to demonstrate the GPl-anchored proteins.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.7.1.3.1.1) [Rodak 2020, p347-354]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 308 · boc2 PDF page 3

question:
Which of the following test results are consistent with a diagnosis of paroxysmal nocturnal
hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
options: decreased conversion of NADH to NAO
explanation:
Blood cell membranes are missing GPl-anchored proteins, ie, CD55 and CD59.
lmmunophenotyping by flow cytometry shows diminished staining for CD55.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.7.1.3.1.1) [Rodak 2020, p347-354)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 309 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is a marker found on:
explanation:
Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is a marker for precursor B and T-cell ALL.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.10.12) [Rodak 2020, p483]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 310 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: In which of the following types of cells is CD5 usually expressed?
explanation:
CD surface markers that identify mature (post-thymic) T cells include CDS.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.12) [Rodak 2020, p483)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 311 · boc2 PDF page 4

question:
Bone marrow examination reveals a hypercellular marrow consisting of probable
lymphoblasts. The cells are positive for TdT, CD3 and CD?; however, the lymphoblasts
are negative for surface immunoglobulins, CD19, and CD10 (CALLA). The most likely
diagnosis is:
explanation:
T-cell markers include CD34, CO2, CD3, CD4, CDS, CD7, CD8 and TOT. B-cell markers
include CD34, CD10, CD19, HLA-DR,TDT, and surface immunoglobulin.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.10.12) [Rodak 2020, p347-354)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 312 · boc2 PDF page 4

question:
A cell surface marker that is expressed on neoplastic plasma cells and is helpful in the
diagnosis of myeloma is:
explanation:
CD138, or kappa and lambda clonal excess, is useful in delineating malignant plasma
cells from a reactive process. Multiple myeloma is a bone marrow based disease in which
plasma cells are found in the marrow. This disorder also presents with a monoclonial protein
or M spike, representing the immunoglobin portion of protein electrophoresis.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.6.2.4) [Rodak 2020, p619-620)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 313 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: Which of the following markers are usually negative in hairy cell leukemia?
explanation:
Hairy cells are mature B lymphocytes that are positive for CD markers CD19, CD20,
CD22, CD25, CD11c, CD103, surface immunoglobulin and TRAP. CDS is a T-cell marker.
[QCMLS 2021 : 4.9.6.1.3] [Rodak 2020, p611-612]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 314 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: Which of the following markers is expressed in most cases of AML?
explanation:
CD117 is one of several markers that will be positive in most cases of AML.
Others include CD13, CD15, CD33 and CD64.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.1.2, 14.9) [Rodak 2020, p483]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 315 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: What feature do CD markers define in a cell?
explanation:
Clusters of differentiation (CD) markers are cellular antigens. Most are determined by flow
cytometry and are instrumental in determining the particular cell's lineage in a blood disorder.
(QCMLS 2021: 4.10.12] [McKenzie 2020, p998)
J. Molecular and Cytogenetic Testing
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 316 · boc2 PDF page 4

question: Which of the following conditions is most often associated with the V617F mutation of JAK2?
explanation:
The specific JAK2 mutation is detected in 95% of patients with polycythemia vera (PV),
which is a myleloproliferative neoplasm with elevations seen in all 3 cell lines.
[QCMLS 2021: 14.11] [Rodak 2020, p565-572]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 317 · boc2 PDF page 5

question:
The t(8;14) chromosomal translocation brings which of the following 2 genes in close
~v proximity?
options: core binding factor alpha and the retinoic acid receptor
the Abelson tyrosine kinase and breakpoint cluster region
c-myc and the immunoglobulin heavy chain
core binding factor beta and the myosin heavy chain
explanation:
The t(8;14) typically found in Burkitt leukemia brings the master cell cycle control factor
c-myc on chromosome 8 under the influence of the strong immunoglobulin heavy chain
promoter on chromosome 14, driving a leukemogenic process.
[QCMLS 2021: 4.9.7.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 318 · boc2 PDF page 5

question:
Which condition is associated with the BCR/ABL gene rearrangement and responds well to
treatment with tyrosine kinase inhibitors?
explanation:
The BCRIABL gene rearrangement is seen in CML. Use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors
results in prolonged survival in most patients with this leukemia and is the first treatment
option, except in pregnant patients.
[QCMLS 4.9.3.1.2.1; 14.11] [McKenzie 2020, p528]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 319 · boc2 PDF page 5

question:
This AML with recurrent cytogenetic abnormality often presents with disseminated
intravascular coagulation:
explanation:
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is often the presenting condition in
patients eventually diagnosed with the 1(15; 17) translocation. This AML is also known
as acute promyelocytic leukemia. Most patients respond well to targeted therapy with
all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA).
[QCMLS 4.9.1.2; 14.9]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 4 · Question 320 · boc2 PDF page 5

question: Vasoconstriction is caused by several regulatory molecules, which include:
explanation:
Thromboxane A2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction. Serotonin released
from the dense bodies of platelets is a vasoconstrictor that binds endothelial cells and platelet
membranes.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.2.1) [Rodak 2020, p143, 631]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 1 · boc2 PDF page 36

question:
Warfarin is classified as a vitamin K antagonist. The factors that are impacted by warfarin
therapy are:
explanation:
Warfarin interferes with the carboxylation of vitamin K factors by interrupting the
enzymatic phase of the reaction. Factors are inhibited according to their half life, with VII
having the shortest (6 hours) and II the longest (2-3 days).
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.5.1.1] (Rodak 2020, p748-749]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 2 · boc2 PDF page 36

question: When a patient is placed on warfarin therapy, the first factor that will be decreased is:
explanation:
Factor VII (proconvertin) is a single-chain glycoprotein that is vitamin-K-dependent
and remains stable for 6 hours in blood. Produced in the liver, it has the shortest half-life;
therefore, it is the first factor affected when a vitamin K antagonist such as warfarin is
administered. FIi has the longest half-life (2-3) days and FVIII is not impacted by warfarin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.5.1.1) [Rodak 2020, p748-749]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 3 · boc2 PDF page 36

question:
A patient with a positive family history of bleeding presents to the ED with the results shown
in this table:
test
result
reference range
aPTT
29.5 seconds
25-35 seconds
PT
19.2 seconds
10.5-12.5 seconds
The patient is not on any medication and so is likely to be deficient in factor:
explanation:
The extrinsic pathway is initiated by the release of tissue thromboplastin that has been
expressed after damage to a vessel. During this process factor VII forms a complex with
tissue thromboplastin and calcium. The PT will be abnormal with deficiencies in the factors
found in both the extrinsic (FVII) and common pathways (I. 11, V and X) and the aPTT is
abnormal when there are deficiencies in the intrinsic pathway (FVIII, FIX, FXI and FXII).
Deficiencies in the intrinsic pathway prevent the activation of factor X in the common pathway
resulting in a prolongation of the aPTT. Factors II and V are found in the common pathway,
and factor VIII is in the intrinsic pathway. Since the aPTT is normal in this case, the likely
deficiency is in factor VII.
(QCMLS 2021 : 5.6.1.2) [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p9, 176)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 4 · boc2 PDF page 36

question: Hageman factor (XII) is involved in each of the following reactions except:
options: activation of C1 to C1 esterase
explanation:
Factor XII is a contact factor, which is activated to factor Xlla. Factor Xlla is responsible
for the activation of factor XI to factor Xia and the conversion of plasminogen to plasm in.
Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin by the action of thrombin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.3, 15.3) [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p10, 35]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 5 · boc2 PDF page 36

question: The most potent plasminogen activator in the contact phase of coagulation is:
explanation:
A clot is degraded by plasmin in the fibrinolytic system. Plasminogen is the zymogen
produced when factor Xlla and kallikrein are produced by contact activation.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.4) [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p48)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 6 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: The activation of plasminogen to plasmin resulting in the degradation of fibrin occurs by:
explanation:
The dissolution of clots occurs several hours after the clot is formed and the key
component is plasminogen. This is converted to plasmin through TPA. This substance is
released as a result of the activity of endothelial damage and the production of thrombin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.4, 15.4)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 7 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: How does tissue factor pathway inhibitor inhibit coagulation?
options: inhibition of tissue factor-factor VI la-factor Xa complex
uncoupling factor XIII dependent crosslinking of fibrin
binding and hiding tissue factor on the endothelial surface
explanation:
TFP1 , also known as extrinsic pathway inhibitor, functions predominantly by inhibiting
the critical first step of coagulation, the formation of the tissue factor-factor VIia-factor Xa
complex.
(QCMLS 2021 : 5.4.2, 15.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 8 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: An inhibitor of plasmin activity is:
explanation:
Alpha-2 antiplasmin is synthesized in the liver and is the primary inhibitor of free plasmin.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.4, 15.4] [Rodak 2020, p644]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 9 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: Antithrombin inhibits factors:
explanation:
AT is a serine protease inhibitor that bin_ds and neutralizes serine proteases, including
thrombin (FIia) and factors IXa, Xa, Xia, and Xlla.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.2.1] (Rodak 2020, p642]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 10 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: The propagation phase of the in vivo coagulation model includes:
options: activation of factor Va and factor VIiia
explanation:
During propagation, 95% of thrombin generation occurs. In the initiation phase, platelets
are activated by the low levels of thrombin that are generated, and adhere to exposed
collagen. The cofactors Va and VIiia are activated by thrombin during the initiation phase.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.4.3] [Rodak 2020, p640]
~ - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 11 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: In the cell-based model of coagulation the intrinsic pathway operates on the:
options: activated platelet surface to produce the burst of thrombin
tissue factor bearing cell to initiate and amplify coagulation
explanation:
In the cell based model of coagulation, the extrinsic or tissue factor pathway operates on
the tissue factor-bearing cell and the intrinsic pathway as occurring on the platelet surface.
(QCMLS 2021 : 5.4.3] [Rodak 2020, p640]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 12 · boc2 PDF page 37

question:
A new oral anticoagulant apixaban has been given to a patient who was previously on
warfarin. This drug directly inhibits:
explanation:
Apixaban is an oral direct anti-FXa inhibitor used to prevent VTE. Direct thrombin
inhibitors will inhibit factor Ila, vitamin K antagonists inhibit the vitamin-K-dependent factors,
while LMWH can inhibit both Ila and Xa.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.7.5.1.2] [Rodak 2020, p747-754]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 13 · boc2 PDF page 37

question: The anticoagulant that directly inhibits thrombin is:
explanation:
Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor that reversibly binds and inactivated free and
clot-bound thrombin. LMWH will inhibit both factor Ila and Xa, whereas warfarin inhibits
vitamin-K-dependent factors. Rivorxaban is an oral direct anti-Xa inhibitor.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.5.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p757-758]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 14 · boc2 PDF page 37

question:
A patient who presents with renal impairment is being started on oral anticoagulant therapy.
The DOAC that should be avoided would be:
Ml s
explanation:
The drug dabigatran is cleared by the kidneys with a half-life of 12-17 hours; however, in
renal disease the half-life may be prolonged up to 60 hours and cause an overdose. Apixaban
and rivaroxaban is only partially eliminated by the kidney, warfarin is eliminated hepatically.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.5.1.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p756-757]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 15 · boc2 PDF page 38

question:
In secondary hemostasis, coagulation proteins become activated to form a fibrin clot. Prior to
these proteins being activated, their inactive proenzymes are known as:
explanation:
In secondary hemostasis, serine proteases are activated to form a fibrin clot. These
proenzymes circulate as zymogens. Zymogens are an inactive protein precursor of an
enzyme converted into an active form.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.4.1, 15.2] [Rodak 2020, p631-632]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 16 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: Alpha granules are found on the platelet in the:
explanation:
The peripheral zone is associated with platelet adhesion and aggregation. The sol-gel
zone provides a cytoskeletal system. The organelle zone contains alpha, dense, and
lysosome granules. Membranes contain the dense tubular system.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.3.1, f5.1]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 17 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: Which of the following best represents the 3 steps of normal hemostasis (in order)?
options: decreased heart rate, adhesion of platelets, plug formation
platelet aggregation, formation of FXIII, fibrin plug
explanation:
Initially vascular damage is met with the body's reaction of "clamping down" to avoid
further blood loss. This usually takes the form of vasoconstriction. In response platelets
adhere to vessels and then aggregate with each other. The primitive platelet plug is then
replaced by the fibrin clot produced through the action of the clotting cascade.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.1, 5.3.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 18 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: Which of the following platelet antigens is the receptor for collagen?
explanation:
All of the glycoprotein complexes are receptors for extracellular antigens. GPlbN/IX is the
vWF receptor, GPllb/llla is the fibrinogen receptor, and GPla/lla is the collagen receptor.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.3.3, f5.2, 15.1] (Kottke-Marchant 2016, p20-21]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 19 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: Which platelet surface antigen acts as the receptor for fibrinogen?
explanation:
The GPlbN/IX complex (CD42) serves as the receptor for platelet adhesion by binding
with von Willebrand factor (vWF). This is followed by GPllb/llla which assists with platelet
aggregation through the binding of fibrinogen. Deficiencies in GPlb lead to Bernard-Soulier
syndrome while a mutation of GPllb/llla accounts for the weakened ("thrombasthenia")
platelet binding in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.3.3, f5.2, 15.1] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p22-23, 213-218]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 20 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: How does GPlb become activated in vivo and in vitro, respectively?
explanation:
GPlb along with GPV/IX acts as a receptor for vWF on the exposed basement membrane
of the endothelium. Shear forces from the circulation activate GPlb in vivo. Ristocetin is an
antibiotic with the side effect of promoting platelet adhesion and will activate GP1 b in vitro.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.3.3] [Kottke-Marchant 2016, p20]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 21 · boc2 PDF page 38

question:
A patient is on aspirin 100 mg/day to prevent the formation of clots caused by platelets.
The mechanism in which aspirin impairs platelet function is by:
options: inactivating cyclooxygenase which blocks thromboxane A2
impairs vWF by via GPlb/lXN receptor
inactivation of ADP and phospholipase A2
explanation:
The acetylation of aspirin inactivates cyclooxygenase, which blocks thromboxane A2
production, which causes impaired platelet function.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.5.2.1, 15.13]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 22 · boc2 PDF page 38

question: A patient is diagnosed with a factor V Leiden mutation. The factor V activity level should be:
explanation:
The Factor V Leiden mutation has no effect on the procoagulant activity of Factor V.
The activity of FV should be within the reference range.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.7.2.4] [Rodak 2020, p728]
- - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 23 · boc2 PDF page 38

question:
The International Sensitivity Index (ISi) is determined by comparing the PT results of the
manufacturer's reagent against:
explanation:
Human brain thromboplastin is the most sensitive of reagents and assigned an ISi of 1.0.
Manufacturers compare their reagents to the most sensitive reagent to determine their
reagents ISi. Micronized silica is an activator in aPTT reagents, rabbit thromboplastin is a type
of PT reagent.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p750)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 24 · boc2 PDF page 39

question:
A coagulation reagent should be sensitive to factor deficiencies. A reagent is considered
sensitive to a factor when the level of factor activity is approximately:
explanation:
A coagulation reagent is considered sensitive to a factor deficiency if it is prolonged when
a patient's factor level is less than 30%, this is the level that will cause most patients to bleed.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.8.2.3] [Rodak 2020, p749]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 25 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: What factors are considered heat labile?
explanation:
Factors V and VIII are considered heat labile and are not stable.
[QCMLS 2021: t.5.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 26 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: What factor serves as a carrier for factor VIII?
explanation:
vWF serves as a carrier for factor VIII. It protects FVIII in circulation and it co-localizes
FVIII at the cite of vascular injury.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.5.2.3] [Rodak 2020, p659]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 27 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: Patients may present with either a bleeding or a thrombotic event in:
explanation:
In a dysfibrinogenemia, the fibrinogen molecule is dysfunctional and can cause either
clotting or bleeding. In hypofibrinogenemia patients present with low fibrinogen, and
in a fibrinogenemia patients have absent fibrinogen, both are at a risk for bleeding. In
hyperfibrinogenemia, there are elevated levels of fibrinogen, if these levels are persistently
high it could put a patient at a risk for thrombosis.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.1.3]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 28 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: The key enzyme of the fibrinolytic system is:
explanation:
Plasmin if the key enzyme responsible for the breakdown of clots. Thrombin is the
key enzyme in the formation of clots. Both urokinase and streptokinase are activators of
fibrinolysis.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.4.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 29 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: The major serine protease responsible for clot breakdown is:
explanation:
Tissue plasminogen activator is a serine protease that catalyzes the conversion of
plasminogen to plasmin and is responsible for clot breakdown. Alpha-2 antiplasmin inactivates
plasmin and plasminogen activator inhibitor inhibits the plasminogen activators. Streptokinase
is a fibrinolytic used to breakdown clots.
[QCMLS 2021 : 5.4.4]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 30 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: What subendothelial structural protein triggers coagulation through activation of FVII?
explanation:
Factor VII is activated in the coagulation cascade by tissue factor. Silica is an activator for
the aPTT.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.4.2]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 31 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: Protein C and its cofactor protein S proteolytically inactivate factors:
explanation:
Factor Va and VIiia inactivation leads to a thrombotic condition. Factors Ila and Xa are
inactivated by AT.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.7.2.2]
II. Disease States
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 32 · boc2 PDF page 39

question: Arterial thrombosis is caused by:
explanation:
Activated platelets, monocytes, and macrophages become embedded within fatty plaque
combining with vWF to form arterial platelet plugs resulting in "white" thrombi seen in arterial
thrombosis, while venous thrombosis is caused by fibrin and RBC.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.7.1.2) [Rodak 2020, p721)
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 33 · boc2 PDF page 40

question: The 2 factors that differentiate liver disease from vitamin K deficiency are:
explanation:
Factors V and VII are helpful in distinguishing between liver disease and vitamin K
deficiency. FVII is a vitamin-K-dependent factor; however, FV is not and will not be decreased
with a vitamin K deficiency. Both factors will be decreased in liver disease.
(QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.4) [Rodak 2020, p654]
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 34 · boc2 PDF page 40

question:
In a patient diagnosed with liver disease, which one of the following factors typically shows an
increase?
explanation:
Liver disease causes a decrease in all factors produced in the liver (factors 11, V, VII, IX,
and X); since FVIII is predominantly produced in endothelial cells, it is not decreased. It also
is an acute phase reactant that may be elevated in liver disease.
[QCMLS 2021: 5.6.2.2] [Rodak 2020, p654]
- - - - - -
source: BOC Study Guide 7e (2022) · Chapter 5 · Question 35 · boc2 PDF page 40

question:
A 4-year-old boy presents with chronic ear infections and is on prophylactic antibiotics. He
also presents with a bleeding diathesis. Factor assay results are shown in this table:
test
